title: What is Knotarium?
text: Knotarium is self-hosted workflow automation that you build by drawing. Instead of writing a script that calls an API, checks a result and sends an email, you place those three steps on a canvas, connect them, and press Run. The result is something you can watch execute, step through afterwards, version, and hand to someone else.

title: The shape of the product
text: Everything is one program. A single .NET process serves the API and the user interface, and stores its data in one local SQLite file. There is no database server to install, no Node.js runtime, no message broker, and no cloud account. You can run it from a folder, as a Windows service, or as a container, and the whole thing is a few hundred megabytes on disk. That matters most when things go wrong: there is exactly one process to restart, one file to back up, and one log to read.

title: The vocabulary
text: Five words carry most of the meaning in this documentation, and they are worth pinning down before anything else. A workflow is nodes joined by edges. One execution of it is a run. Workflow — the graph you draw. It is the unit you save, publish, share and enable. Node — one step. Sending an HTTP request, querying a database, branching on a condition, writing a log line. Edge — a connection from one node's output to the next node's input. Edges carry both the flow of control and the data. Trigger — what starts a run: a manual click, a schedule, an inbound webhook, a poller that watches a source

title: The logic is real C#, compiled as it runs
text: The Inline Code node and custom node packages are genuine C# compiled at runtime, not a scripting dialect bolted on for configuration. That is a real capability and a real risk, which is why code execution is switched off until an administrator turns it on.

title: You can step backwards through a finished run
text: Because every run is journaled node by node, the inspector can show you what each node received, what it produced, and what the variables looked like immediately before and after it ran — for a run that finished days ago. When a workflow misbehaves you are reading a recording, not reproducing a bug.

title: AI output passes through deterministic gates
text: Alongside the usual prompt and routing nodes, two nodes turn a language model's answer into structured findings that ordinary code then judges. A claim with no supporting evidence is marked unsupported rather than being quietly accepted. The decision to continue is made by your rule, not by asking a model whether it thinks it did well.

title: Dangerous things are off until you switch them on
text: File access is denied by default and granted one directory at a time. Code execution and database access are disabled until enabled explicitly. Outbound requests are checked against an egress policy that blocks internal addresses. Importing a workflow that contains a privileged node asks you to acknowledge it first. Treat a running instance as privileged Knotarium exists to execute code and touch systems on your behalf. Anyone who can reach the interface can eventually make it do those things. title: Install and run

text: Tag Moves when :latest A stable version is tagged — one with no hyphen in it. :edge A pre-release is tagged, meaning a version containing a hyphen such as 1.0.0-rc.15 . :<version> Never. title: Volumes and file ownership
text: The image sets Storage__DataDirectory=/data and declares /data as a volume, so the database and the credential key land there together. It also runs as the base image's non-root user, whose numeric identifier is 1654 , and the image creates /data already owned by that user. That ownership is why a named volume works with no setup: on first initialisation a named volume inherits the ownership of the mount point inside the image. title: Verifying what you downloaded
text: Every release artifact ships with a .sha256 sidecar next to it, generated from the final bytes of the file. The sidecar holds the hash and the filename separated by two spaces, which is the format the standard Unix tool expects. # Windows — compare the output against the .sha256 file Get-FileHash .\Knotarium-<version>-win-x64.zip # Linux — verify against the sidecar directly sha256sum -c Knotarium-<version>-linux-x64.tar.gz.sha256 When the release pipeline signs artifacts, it regenerates the checksums afterwards, because signing changes the file's bytes and the pre-signing hash would be stale.

title: Upgrading
text: The database schema is created and migrated on startup, so no upgrade path has a manual migration step. What differs is how the old files are replaced.

title: Windows installer
text: Run the new installer over the old one. The application identifier is deliberately stable across versions, so an upgrade replaces the installation rather than sitting beside it. Before copying any file the installer stops the service and polls until it genuinely reports stopped — up to 45 seconds, because sc stop returns immediately while the application is still draining in-flight runs. It then deletes the service, force-terminates any surviving process including the sandbox worker child, replaces the files, and recreates and starts the service. That polling exists because a fixed short wait

title: Container
text: docker pull ghcr.io/andrekfm/knotarium:latest docker rm -f knotarium docker run -d --name knotarium -p 43120 :43120 \ -v knotarium-data:/data ghcr.io/andrekfm/knotarium:latest Removing and recreating the container is the upgrade. The volume is untouched by both operations, which is where all of your state lives.

title: Linux
text: Stop the service, replace the contents of /opt/knotarium with the new release, restore the executable bit and the ownership, and start it again. Leave /var/lib/knotarium alone — that is the data, and nothing about an upgrade should touch it.

title: Uninstalling
text: The Windows uninstaller stops and deletes the service and removes the program files, but leaves %ProgramData%\Knotarium in place so that reinstalling keeps your workflows. If you want a genuinely clean machine, delete that directory yourself afterwards. The same principle applies on Linux: removing the unit and /opt/knotarium leaves /var/lib/knotarium untouched.

title: Core concepts
text: This page names the moving parts and explains how they relate. It is the page the rest of the manual leans on: once you know what a version is, what arms a trigger, and how one node reads another's output, most of the interface stops needing explanation. Read it after you have run something once — the vocabulary lands better with a run behind you.

title: Workflows, nodes and edges
text: A workflow is a directed graph. In code it is a WorkflowDefinition : an identifier, a name, a list of nodes, a list of edges, and a little metadata. Two booleans ride along — whether it is enabled, and whether it has been archived — and both are covered below. A node is one step. Structurally it is almost nothing: an identifier, a type string naming which node package it is, and an untyped bag of properties. Everything you configure in the property inspector lands in that bag. Position is a property, not a field A node's place on the canvas is not part of the graph model. Coordinates, size and

Most nodes declare a single output called result and behave like a straight line. The interesting ones do not. title: Expressions
text: Nodes pass data to each other through expressions written in double braces. There is no general scripting language here — the evaluator is a small hand-written parser with a fixed grammar, which is deliberate: expressions are configuration, and configuration that can do anything is a security problem.

title: The two reference forms
text: There are exactly two rooted references. Everything else is a literal, an operator or one of four functions. # Read an earlier node's output {{ $node .<node-id>.output.<field> }} # Read a variable {{ $variables .<name> }} The field part is a path, not just a name. It walks into nested objects with dots, indexes arrays with brackets, and accepts quoted keys when a key contains something awkward: {{ $node.fetch-user.output.success }} {{ $node.fetch-user.output.payload.user.name }} {{ $node.fetch-user.output.payload.user.roles[ 0 ] }} {{ $node.n1.output.result[ "a key with spaces" ] }} Why node i

title: What the grammar supports
text: Comparison with == and != , arithmetic with + , - , * and / , boolean && and || , parentheses, and string, number, boolean and null literals. The + operator concatenates when either side is a string. Division by zero yields zero rather than failing. Four functions are allowed, and the names are matched case-insensitively: Function Returns now() The current UTC time in round-trip format. uuid() A fresh identifier. coalesce(a, b, …) The first argument that is neither null nor an empty string. length(x) String length, array length, or a collection count; zero otherwise. Anything else is refused o

text: This distinction matters more than it looks. When a field contains nothing but a single expression, the result keeps its type — a number stays a number, an object stays an object. When the expression is mixed with any surrounding text, every value is converted to a string and concatenated. # Passes a real number through {{ $node.calc.output.result }} # Passes the string "Total: 42" Total: {{ $node.calc.output.result }} A downstream node expecting a number and receiving "42" is a common and confusing failure. title: Variables
text: A variable is a named value living in a bag attached to one run . The Set Variable node writes to it; expressions and nodes read from it. Variables do not survive the run that created them There is no workflow-level or instance-level variable store. The bag is created when a run starts and is discarded with it. A workflow that needs to remember something between runs must write it somewhere real — a file, a database, an external service. This surprises people coming from tools with persistent workflow state. Reads resolve in three steps: a direct key in the bag, then a dotted path into a struc

title: Secrets are not variables
text: Passwords, tokens and API keys live in a separate credential store, encrypted at rest. A node does not receive a secret through a variable; it holds a reference , and the engine resolves the reference at the moment of use. This is what makes a workflow safe to export: the exported file names the credential slot it needs, never the secret itself.

title: Runs and journaling
text: One execution of a workflow is a run . It records which workflow and which version it used, when it started, what started it, its variable bag, and a status. Status Meaning Pending Queued, not started. Running In progress. Suspended Paused awaiting something external. WaitingForRetry A node failed and will be retried. Completed Finished successfully. The timeline labels this Success . Failed Finished unsuccessfully. Cancelled Stopped deliberately, including by disabling the workflow. Discarded A failed run triaged away in the dead-letter view and no longer treated as actionable. Each node in t

title: Replay is a new run
text: Replaying picks a node as a cut point. The engine creates a brand-new run that inherits the recorded state of everything upstream of that node and re-executes the cut point and everything downstream of it. The original run is never modified — it stays as evidence, and the two are linked so you can navigate between them. Because downstream nodes really do run again, replay warns you about any of them that perform a non-idempotent side effect. Sending an email twice is a decision, not an accident, so the engine makes you take it knowingly.

title: Drafts, versions and activation
text: This is the concept people most often get wrong, and it has three states, not two. Three states, two transitions. Publishing normally performs both. The draft is what the canvas edits. It is stored as an indented JSON file on disk rather than in the database — deliberately, so that drafts are readable and can be kept under version control alongside other configuration. Publishing compiles the draft and, if it compiles cleanly, freezes it as a numbered, immutable version in the database. If compilation fails, nothing is written at all and you get the diagnostics instead. Publishing an unchanged

title: The draft never executes
text: This is the part that trips people up, and it is worth stating flatly: every run executes the active version — a manual click included. There is no execution path that reads the graph you are currently editing. The endpoint that starts a run rebuilds the workflow from the active version's nodes and edges, and refuses outright when no version is active. Pressing Run in the editor therefore does two things in order: it activates the version chosen in the toolbar's runtime-version picker, and only then starts a run. The button's tooltip says so — Activate the selected version and run it. On a wor

title: Where versions come from
text: Origin Created by Published Publishing the current draft. Restored Restoring an earlier version, which copies it forward as a new version rather than reviving the old one. Imported Importing an external definition. Imported versions arrive inactive. Restoring never mutates history. Version 3 restored from version 1 becomes version 4, and versions 1 through 3 remain exactly as they were. Deleting a workflow is likewise a soft delete: archiving removes the editable draft but keeps the version history and the activation log intact, because the ability to explain a past run outlives the workflow i

title: Enabled, and armed
text: Two independent switches decide whether anything happens on its own. Both must be on, and they fail in the same silent way when they are not.

title: Enabled — per workflow
text: The enabled flag gates automatic and external starts for one workflow: schedules, polling triggers, inbound webhook and external calls, and an AI Agent's ability to invoke it as a tool. Manual runs are not gated by it. That exemption is about being allowed to start , not about what gets executed — a manual run on a disabled workflow still runs the active published version, exactly like every other run. Disabling is more forceful than it sounds. As well as stopping new runs, it cancels runs already in flight — every pending, running, suspended or retry-waiting execution is set to cancelled and

title: Armed — per instance
text: Arming is a single global switch separating design time from run time. While disarmed, schedule evaluation and polling are skipped entirely, inbound device signals are dropped, and externally triggered runs are refused. Manual runs always execute. A fresh install starts disarmed . Once an instance has run, the stored state wins over configuration. The disk guard disarms and never re-arms A background check samples free disk space. When it drops below the configured floor and the runtime is armed, the runtime disarms itself and logs a critical message. Freeing space does not bring it back — re-

title: Capabilities and the security posture
text: A node package declares the privileged things it touches as capability tags — reading files, writing files, executing code, querying a database, making network calls, resolving credentials, running an agent loop. Declaring a tag is metadata. Only some of them are enforced , and the distinction matters. Capability Enforced how Default code.execute Instance-wide toggle Off database Instance-wide toggle Off aiAgent Instance-wide toggle Off filesystem.read Per-directory file access policy Denied filesystem.write Per-directory file access policy Denied network Not gated by this system — see below —

title: Sub-flows
text: A sub-flow lets one workflow be used as a step inside another. The calling graph contains a Subflow node naming the workflow to include. Sub-flows are inlined, not called Despite the vocabulary, there is no runtime call and no child run. At compile time the referenced graph is spliced into the parent, producing one flat execution plan. There is one run, one timeline, and one set of node states covering both graphs. Recursion is not a stack overflow at runtime — it is a compile error. Inlining renames the child's nodes with a prefix so that including the same sub-flow twice produces two indepen

title: Templates and bundles
text: Both are ways of moving work between instances, and they differ in scope. A template is a single workflow with metadata, packaged as a zip with a .kgtpl extension containing exactly two entries: a manifest and the workflow document. It is a secret-free projection — credentials it needs are declared as named slots that the installer asks you to bind to real credentials on your instance. A template can also declare parameters, substituted into the graph at install time. A bundle is bigger: several workflows plus the node packages they depend on, with a .kgbundle extension. It carries two files t

Untrusted Anything else, including an unrecognised trust token. Never. The rule the trust model exists to enforce is that a package claiming a remote or official origin without a signature that verifies against a trusted key must not be trusted. Unknown values fail closed to untrusted rather than being treated optimistically. Templates carry no signature at all, which is part of why they are limited to a si

title: The canvas editor
text: The canvas is where a workflow is drawn: nodes on the left, the graph in the middle, the selected node's properties on the right. This page covers the parts of that screen that are not obvious from looking at it — how wiring actually behaves, which gestures are destructive, what the layout tools do to your positions, and the one side effect of opening the editor that surprises everybody.

title: Opening the editor
text: There are two ways in, and they do different things. Opening a workflow from the dashboard loads that workflow. Clicking Canvas Editor in the header always starts a new, empty workflow containing a single Start node — it does not return you to whatever you had open. Coming back to a workflow you were editing means going through the dashboard again. The editor remembers where you were looking. The viewport (pan and zoom) is stored per workflow in browser storage, so re-entering a graph lands where you left it rather than re-centring. If the stored viewport would leave the graph off screen — whi

title: The node palette
text: Nodes are grouped into six categories — Trigger, Logic, Data, Network, AI and Utility — derived from each node package's declared category. Above them sits a Recent / Pinned panel, and below them a Templates panel and a collapsed Advanced panel. Advanced holds nodes whose manifest marks them as escape hatches; it starts collapsed so the ordinary building blocks are the obvious choice. The search box filters on what you can actually read on the card: the node's display name, its description and its category. It deliberately does not match the internal node id, because matching ids produced resu

title: Placing nodes
text: Clicking a palette entry drops the node at an automatically chosen position. Dragging it onto the canvas places it exactly where you release, which is almost always what you want, because several placement behaviours key off where the node lands: Dropped on an existing wire , the node is spliced into that connection: the wire is cut and re-routed through the new node, as a single undo step. Dropped into a loop or parallel container , the node becomes a child of that container and moves with it. If the container was empty and the node is not a trigger, it is auto-wired from the container's star

title: Connecting nodes
text: A connection always runs from an output port on the left-hand node to an input port on the right-hand one. There are three ways to make one, and they exist because dragging precisely onto a small dot is hard on a trackpad and impossible on a touch screen. Drag between ports. The drop is magnetic within roughly seventy pixels, so you do not have to hit the dot exactly. Drag onto the node. Releasing anywhere over a target node connects to that node's first input port. Click, then click. Click an output port, then click either an input port or anywhere on the target node. Clicking empty canvas or

title: Selecting and moving
text: Left-dragging on empty canvas draws a selection box, and a node only has to be touched by that box to be selected. Panning is on the middle and right mouse buttons. Shift or Ctrl adds to a selection, and Ctrl + A selects every node. Clicking a node also pins its data wires on (see the density control below), which is why a single click makes dashed lines appear. Double-clicking has a per-type meaning: a Sub-flow node drills into the workflow it calls, an Inline Code node opens the code editor, and a Condition node opens the full-screen logic editor. Double-clicking anywhere else zooms.

title: The property inspector
text: The upper right panel configures whatever is selected. Its header shows the node's display name and its node id — worth noting, because that id is what expressions reference — plus a delete button. The form itself is generated from the node package's manifest, so the fields you see are the fields that node actually declares; a few node types (HTTP Request, Scheduler, Polling Trigger, Resource Picker, imported OpenAPI operations, Sub-flow) render a purpose-built form instead. Above the form, two sections appear when they have something to offer. Insert data reference lists the outputs of every

title: Align, distribute and Tidy
text: The floating toolbar at the top right of the canvas holds the layout tools. Alignment buttons appear once two nodes are selected (left, horizontal centres, right, top, vertical centres, bottom); distribution buttons appear at three (horizontal, vertical). Both apply as a single undo step. Tidy re-lays the entire graph left to right and then re-frames the view. It is container-aware: the body of each loop or parallel container is arranged inside its container, and a container is never shrunk below its current size. Because it moves every node it is one undo step, and undo puts every position ba

title: The data-wire density control
text: Reading a variable does not draw a normal edge, because the value does not travel along the control flow — it is fetched from the workflow's variable store. The editor still shows those reads, as dashed wires between the node that produced a variable and each node that consumes it. Because a busy graph can have a great many of them, the eye button at the bottom right of the canvas chooses how much is drawn. Mode What is drawn Reveal on demand Default Only the execution flow. Data wires appear when you hover or click a node or a variable. Compact dots Dashed data wires always visible, each coll

title: Sticky notes and groups
text: Both are editor-only annotations. They have no ports, are registered on the backend as no-ops so they survive save, publish, versioning and restore like any other node, and they never execute. Note on the toolbar drops a sticky note at the centre of the current view, selected and ready to type into. A selected note can be resized (down to 140 by 90 pixels) and recoloured from five swatches. In a read-only view the text is shown but cannot be edited. Group appears once two or more nodes are selected and wraps them in a tinted frame. A group is purely visual — it does not change execution — but

title: Finding a node
text: Ctrl + F or Ctrl + K ( ⌘ on macOS) opens a jump palette that filters the nodes on the canvas by title. Arrow keys move through the results, Enter jumps to the highlighted one, and Esc closes. Picking a result centres the canvas on that node at a fixed zoom and selects it, which also brings its properties up on the right. This shortcut is allowed even while a text field has focus, so it can always be summoned; once open, the palette owns the keyboard.

title: Undo and redo
text: Every structural edit records a snapshot before it happens, and compound gestures collapse into one step: a drag that moves a node, a drop that also auto-connects, a Tidy that moves fifty nodes, an extraction that rewrites the graph. A drag that does not actually move anything records nothing. The history keeps up to 100 steps in each direction and is reset when a different workflow is loaded — it is not a cross-workflow timeline. Undo and redo are ignored while the cursor is in a text field, so typing in a property field and pressing Ctrl + Z undoes your typing, not your last wire.

title: Leaving with unsaved changes
text: The editor compares the current graph against the last saved state, ignoring things that do not affect the definition. Pressing Back with pending edits opens a dialog offering Cancel , Discard & leave and Save & leave . Closing or reloading the browser tab instead gets the browser's own native "leave site?" prompt. Only the canvas Back button is guarded The dialog is wired to the editor's own Back button. Navigating away with the header tabs — to the dashboard, settings, or anywhere else — leaves the editor without asking, and unsaved canvas edits are lost. Save before switching screens. Editi

title: Read-only version preview
text: Picking an older version in the Runtime version dropdown does not activate it. It opens a read-only preview of that version's graph: an amber banner appears, the canvas is rendered at reduced opacity, and dragging, connecting and selecting are all disabled. Your working draft is untouched underneath and returns when you exit. From the banner you can Diff the previewed version against your draft, or Restore this version , which makes it the current live version and brings its content back into the draft. Restore is hidden when the version you are previewing is already the active one. Esc exits

title: Save & Publish and Run
text: Save & Publish is one action with two effects: it persists the draft, then snapshots it as a runtime version and activates that version, so the workflow is immediately runnable. Identical content is de-duplicated on the backend, so re-saving an unchanged graph does not spawn a new version. The button reads Saved and is disabled when there is nothing new to publish; a workflow that has never been published can always publish its first version. When the graph has blocking errors the button turns amber and reads Save & Publish (2 errors) . It stays clickable on purpose — saving still keeps your d

title: Expressions and data
text: Edges carry control, not values. When a node needs something an earlier node produced, it asks for it by name inside a {{ … }} expression. This page covers the two reference forms that exist, how a path into nested data is written, what happens when a reference does not resolve, and the two design-time tools — the Node I/O inspector and pinned outputs — that let you build a downstream node before the upstream one is finished.

title: The two reference forms
text: There are exactly two roots. Everything else you may have seen in other automation tools — $trigger , $env , $json , $item — does not exist here. # Read a named output field of a specific node {{ $node . fetch-user .output. statusCode }} # Read a variable from the workflow's variable store {{ $variables . customerId }} $node references are addressed by the node id , which is shown under the title in the property inspector — not by the node's display name. The literal .output. in the middle is required; without it the reference resolves to nothing. Node ids containing hyphens are fine. A bare i

title: Reaching into nested data
text: Both forms share one path grammar. The head is everything up to the first . or [ ; after that you may chain member and index segments freely. Segment Means .name A member of an object. ["name"] or ['name'] The same, but the key may contain dots or other awkward characters. [0] An element of an array. The index must be a non-negative whole number. {{ $node.fetch-user.output.payload.user.age }} {{ $node.fetch-user.output.payload [ 0 ] .email }} {{ $variables.config.servers [ 2 ] .host }} {{ $variables.lookup [ "order.id" ] }} Every part of a reference is matched exactly, including case: the node

title: Whole value or interpolated text
text: This distinction decides whether a field receives a real object or a piece of text, and it catches people out. When a field's value is nothing but one expression , the result keeps its type: an object stays an object, an array stays an array, a number stays a number. When the expression is embedded in surrounding text, everything is converted to string and concatenated. Field value Node receives {{ $node.a.output.payload }} The object itself. Order {{ $node.a.output.id }} received A string. {{ $node.a.output.payload }} A string — the leading space makes it interpolation. One stray space change

title: When a reference does not resolve
text: A syntactically valid reference that points at nothing — an unknown node, an output that node never produced, a member that is not there, an array index past the end — does not raise an error. It resolves to nothing, and how that lands depends on the shape of the field: As a whole value , the parameter is null. Embedded in text , it contributes an empty string, so Order {{ … }} received becomes Order received . This is a deliberate design — a run should not die because one optional field was absent — but it means a typo in a reference is silent . A node that suddenly logs a blank where a value

title: More than references
text: The space between the braces is a small expression language, not just a reference slot. It supports string literals in single or double quotes, numbers, true , false and null , parentheses, the arithmetic operators + - * / , the comparisons == and != , and the logical && and || . The + operator concatenates when either side is a string and adds otherwise. Division by zero yields zero rather than failing. Four functions are available, and only these four — anything else is rejected outright: Function Returns now() The current UTC time as a round-trip formatted string. uuid() A fresh identifier.

title: Discovering references in the editor
text: You rarely need to type any of the above by hand. Four affordances produce correct references for you.

title: Autocomplete inside a field
text: Typing {{ in an expression-capable field opens a list of the workflow's known references — promoted node outputs and variables — filtered by whatever you type after the braces. Arrow keys move, Enter or Tab inserts the complete {{ … }} expression, and Esc closes the list.

title: The Insert data reference chips
text: Near the top of the property inspector, a panel titled Insert data reference lists every upstream node — every ancestor, not just the immediate predecessor — grouped by node, with one chip per data field it exposes. Clicking a chip copies the full expression to the clipboard, ready to paste into any field. Control and branch ports such as true and false carry no payload and are left out. On graphs started by an external device or an event or action trigger, a second panel offers the fields that signal carries. Those are scoped to the run rather than shared, which is why they appear per node ra

title: Dragging an output chip
text: Each node card shows its outputs as small draggable pills. Dragging one has two useful destinations: Onto another node — binds that output to the target node's primary input field, as a stored reference rather than as typed text. Onto the Workflow variables panel — promotes the output to a named entry in the variable store, described in Variables . While you drag, a hint reading Drop output into the global store appears at the bottom of the canvas. A promoted output is proposed with the name <nodeId>_<outputName> , which you can rename afterwards. Promoting the same output twice returns the ex

title: The Node I/O inspector
text: At the bottom of the property inspector, the Input / Output section answers "what does this node actually produce?" without leaving the canvas. It loads the workflow's most recent run and shows the selected node's recorded inputs, the variables as they stood, and its outputs. A Refresh button re-reads the latest run. Before a node has ever run there is nothing recorded, and the section says so. It then falls back to the declared outputs from the node package's manifest — each output's name, its type, and the field names it declares — so you can still see the shape of what the node will emit an

title: Pinned outputs
text: Building the third node of a chain usually means running the first two over and over. A pinned output short-circuits that: the node stops executing and returns a sample you supply, so everything downstream can be built and re-run immediately. The Pinned output control sits at the very bottom of the property inspector. Clicking Pin output opens a JSON editor and a port field; the port defaults to result . The payload must be valid JSON — invalid text is reported inline and is not stored. Clear pin removes the pin entirely. A pin only affects manual runs. Everything automatic behaves as if the p

title: Variables
text: A variable is a named value that any node in the workflow can read, regardless of whether it is wired to the node that produced it. Variables are how data reaches a branch that control flow never touched, how a loop accumulates a result, and how a sub-flow hands something back to its caller. This page covers the two nodes that write them, the path syntax for nested writes, what the Variables panel is and — importantly — is not, and how far a variable's lifetime extends.

title: Scope: one run, not one installation
text: The word "global" appears throughout the interface, and it means global within this run . Every execution starts with its own variable bag, seeded by whatever started it, and nothing carries over from the previous run. There is no installation-wide key/value store behind this feature; if you need a value to survive between runs it has to live somewhere real, such as a file or a database. The bag is snapshotted as the run progresses: the run record keeps the final state, and each node's journal entry records the variables as they stood immediately before that node executed. That is what makes t

title: The Set Variable node
text: Set Variable (category Utility) writes one value. It has two fields: Field Expressions Effect variableName No The name to write, or a path into a nested structure. Taken literally — a {{ … }} expression here is not evaluated and becomes part of the name. value Yes The value to store. Evaluated before the node runs, so it may be a literal or any expression. A Set Variable node with an empty name does nothing at all and reports success — it is not an error. Writing null into a plain (non-path) name removes the variable rather than storing a null, which matters if a later node tests for its prese

title: The Set Variables node
text: Set Variables writes several at once from a list of name-and-value rows. It exists so that initialising six values does not need six nodes in a chain. Each row's value is expression-enabled, and each row's name follows the same path rules as the single node. Rows are applied in order, and the rules for a bad row differ depending on what is wrong with it: A row with a missing or blank name is skipped silently. Nothing is written and nothing is reported. A row whose write conflicts structurally with what is already stored fails the node — and the rows before it stay applied . There is no rollbac

title: Writing into a nested path
text: The name field is not restricted to a plain identifier. It accepts the same path grammar used for reading, so a single node can reach into a structure: # Head only — an ordinary variable counter # Member access, two equivalent spellings myDict.name myDict [ "name" ] # Array index list [ 0 ] # Chained freely config.servers [ 2 ] .host The head — everything before the first . or [ — is the variable that actually exists. Writing myDict["name"] creates or updates a variable called myDict ; there is no variable called myDict["name"] .

title: What is created for you
text: Missing containers are built automatically , and their kind is inferred from the next segment: a following index makes an array, anything else makes an object. So config.servers[2].host against a variable that does not exist yet produces an object containing an array containing an object. Arrays grow to fit. An index past the end is not an error — the array is padded with nulls up to that position. Writing list[1] into an empty array gives [null, value] . Siblings survive. Writing myDict["b"] when myDict already holds { "a": 1 } leaves a alone.

title: What fails
text: A write fails when it contradicts the shape already stored — asking for a member of a number, or an index of an object. The node fails with a message naming the variable and the conflict, for example Set Variable 'myVar["a"]': Cannot navigate by member: the variable's current value is not an object. The four conflict messages distinguish navigating by member versus by index, and at the head versus deeper in the path. A malformed path is not an error — it becomes a name If the path cannot be parsed at all — an unterminated bracket, a doubled dot, a negative or non-numeric index, a quoted key th

title: The Variables panel
text: The lower right panel of the canvas, titled Workflow variables , is the editor's view of the store. Each card shows a variable's name, a type sigil, its last known value, the node that produces it and the nodes that consume it. Sigil Type "" string # number ? boolean {} dictionary [] array A variable is either awaiting run or resolved . Running the workflow from the editor fills the resolved values in place, without leaving the canvas.

title: Two kinds of entry
text: Declared entries carry a small declared badge. They are derived automatically from the Set Variable and Set Variables nodes on the canvas — and from a sub-flow's declared inputs and outputs while you are editing it — so they appear and disappear as you edit those nodes. They cannot be renamed or deleted from the panel; edit the node instead. A keyed write contributes its head container, with the object or array glyph inferred from the path syntax and no design-time value. Promoted entries are ones you registered yourself by dragging a node's output pill onto the panel's drop zone. These can be

title: Dropping an output into the store
text: Dragging an output pill from a node card onto the panel's drop zone — labelled Register New Variable , and Drop Node Output Here while you hover — promotes that output to a named variable. The proposed name is <nodeId>_<outputName> . Dropping the same output again returns the existing entry rather than duplicating it. That naming convention is not cosmetic. When a variable cannot be found in the run's bag, the runtime falls back to interpreting its name as nodeId_outputName (split at the last underscore) and reads that node's recorded output directly. This is what makes a promoted output resol

title: Using a variable in a node
text: There are two ways to consume one, and they are not equivalent. Drag the variable pill onto a node. This stores a structured reference on the node's primary input field. At run time it is resolved by looking the name up in the variable bag, including a dotted path into a structured value such as an inbound signal. Type an expression such as {{ $variables.customerId }} into any expression-capable field, as described in Expressions and data . Both work. The difference shows up in the editor: the dashed data wires drawn between a variable's producer and its consumers, and the Consumers list on th

title: Conditions and branching
text: Branching is what turns a sequence of steps into a workflow. Knotarium's main branch node is Condition , which has a dedicated full-screen editor for building nested AND/OR/NOT logic and previewing the result against real data before you ever run anything. This page covers that editor in detail, and then the two other nodes that route a run — Switch and AI Router — including a limitation of Switch that is worth knowing before you build on it.

title: The Condition node
text: The Condition node has two output ports, true and false , and the run follows exactly one of them. It is one of a small, explicit set of node types the engine treats as branch routers: when such a node reports which port it chose, every outgoing edge on a different port is suppressed. Configuration is stored in a single logic property. A much older format kept three separate fields — left , operator and right — and nodes still carrying it continue to run. Precedence at run time is strict: valid logic wins; otherwise the legacy fields are used; a node with neither is a configuration error.

title: The logic editor
text: The property inspector shows a one-line summary of the current logic and an Edit logic button. Double-clicking the Condition node on the canvas opens the same editor. It fills the screen, because a condition of any real complexity does not fit in a side panel. The editor draws the logic as a left-to-right dataflow graph rather than as nested boxes: operand cards on the left feed comparator cards, comparators feed AND/OR group cards and NOT cards, and the final result arrives at a TRUE/FALSE output card on the right. The layout is computed for you — nodes cannot be dragged — and it is recompute

title: Building one comparison
text: Clicking an operand card opens a small editor with two tabs. Reference lists the workflow's variables and, on signal-driven graphs, the fields of the inbound signal, each with its type. Picking one stores an expression that is resolved at run time. Beneath the list is a Sample value field used only by the live preview. Literal offers a string / number / boolean selector. Boolean literals are a true/false toggle rather than free text; the other two are a text field, and the value is converted to its declared type when you save. For the two membership operators the right-hand operand is a list i

title: The operator catalogue
text: The catalogue is shared between the editor and the runtime and is kept in sync by a drift test, so what the menu offers is exactly what will execute. Unary operators ignore the right-hand operand entirely. Group Operators Comparison Equals = , Not equals ≠ , Greater than > , Greater or equal ≥ , Less than < , Less or equal ≤ Text Contains, Does not contain, Starts with, Ends with, Matches regex Membership Is one of, Is not one of — both take a list on the right Existence Is empty, Is not empty, Exists, Does not exist — all unary Boolean Is true, Is false — both unary

title: Type filtering and the ordering guardrails
text: When the left operand's type is known, the operator menu only offers operators that accept it. A number hides the text operators, a boolean hides the ordering operators, and so on. Exists and Does not exist are genuinely type-agnostic and are always offered. When the type is not known — a dynamic reference — everything is offered and the runtime is the backstop. Ordering comparisons are constrained further. If both operand types are known and they differ, or they match but are not orderable, the editor blocks the combination so it can never be saved, with a reason such as Ordering needs matchi

title: Grouping and negation
text: Add condition in the toolbar adds a comparator, wrapping the existing logic in an AND group if it was a bare comparison. Every card carries three small tools: wrap in a group, wrap in NOT, and remove. A group card switches between AND and OR, and groups nest freely, so (A AND B) OR NOT C is built by wrapping, not by typing. The structure has bounds, mirrored from the parser that validates it on the backend: nesting at most 20 deep, at most 200 nodes in the whole tree, and at most 50 children in any one group. A literal may be up to 10,000 characters, a reference 2,000, and a regular expression

title: The live preview
text: Everything in the editor is evaluated as you type. Each comparator card shows its own result, the wires are coloured by what they carry, and an output pill in the toolbar gives the overall verdict. State Means TRUE / FALSE The comparison resolved with the values currently in play. runtime Valid, but referencing something that has no design-time value. It will resolve when the workflow runs. This is a healthy state, not a problem. incomplete An operand or operator is still missing. Save is blocked. error The comparison cannot be evaluated as written — for example a type mismatch or a malformed

title: Where the preview gets its values
text: This is the part that makes the preview trustworthy. When the workflow has already run, the editor asks the backend to resolve each of the condition's references against the last real run , and a Last run / Manual selector appears in the toolbar. Last run is chosen by default. The selector shows when that run happened, and marks it stale when the run came from a different published version than the one you are editing — the values are still shown, but the graph they came from is not this graph. Switching to Manual uses the per-operand Sample value fields instead. If the workflow has never run,

title: Test mode
text: The ▶ Test button turns every reference operand into an editable field so you can type the values an incoming signal would carry and watch the condition resolve. A row of presets fills them for you: make everything match, make one named comparator fail, make everything fail, or clear. The bar states plainly that values are temporary and the configuration is unchanged, and ✕ Exit test discards them.

title: Migrating a legacy condition
text: A node still using the old three-field form is summarised in the property inspector as Legacy condition — open to migrate . Opening the editor seeds a single comparator from those fields as a best effort, and saving writes the new format and deletes the old left , operator and right properties. The migration is one-way and happens on save, not on open, so opening a legacy condition to look at it changes nothing. The editor also opens conditions already stored in the earlier flat format — a list of comparators joined by one combinator — and saves them as a tree. The property inspector renders t

title: What blocks publishing
text: A Condition node is publishable when it can produce a definite branch: it has either a logic blob that parses, or a legacy operator. A node with neither, or whose logic no longer parses, is incomplete and publishing is refused with a message naming the offending node ids and telling you to open and complete them in the editor. Saving a draft is deliberately not gated, so an unfinished condition never stops you from saving work in progress. Only publishing and activating are checked.

title: What happens at run time
text: References inside the logic are resolved by the node itself rather than by the generic expression pass, which lets it distinguish "resolved to null" from "could not be found". The outcome maps onto three behaviours: True or False — the run continues down that port. Error — the node fails , carrying a code and the comparator and operand that caused it. The codes are INVALID_LOGIC , RESOLUTION_FAILED , COERCION_FAILED , TYPE_MISMATCH and an internal-invariant backstop. A node with no configuration at all takes the false port. That is the only silent fallback, and the publish gate is what stops i

title: The Switch node
text: Switch (category Control) takes a value and a cases list. The list is split on commas, semicolons and line breaks; entries are trimmed and empties dropped. At run time the value is compared against each case in order, ignoring case, and the node reports the first case that matched — or default when none did. Switch does not currently branch Two things stop it. Unlike Switch, it is a real branch router: the port it selects is the only one followed. Its branches are not fixed. The categories field takes labels separated by commas, semicolons or line breaks, and each label becomes an output port on the node card as you type , followed always by an otherwise fallback. title: Sub-flows and grouping
text: A sub-flow is an ordinary workflow called as a single step from another one. It is how a chain of nodes that appears in four places becomes one node in four places. This page covers the Sub-flow node, the typed interface a child declares, how data crosses the boundary, the "Extract selection" command and the fairly strict rules it enforces, and why grouping is a different thing entirely.

title: What a sub-flow actually is
text: This is worth understanding before anything else, because it explains most of the behaviour that follows. A sub-flow is not a separate run. When the workflow is compiled, the child's nodes are copied into the parent's execution plan, the Sub-flow node itself disappears, and the wires that led into it are redirected to the child's Start node while the wires that led out of it come from the child's End node. The consequences are concrete. There is no child execution to inspect separately — the child's steps appear in the parent's run, with ids like my-subflow-node/step-2 . There is no "run async

title: Adding a Sub-flow node
text: Drop a Subflow node (category Control) onto the canvas. It has one input and a single result output. Its property panel offers a searchable list of every other workflow — the workflow you are editing is excluded, since a node cannot call its own graph — and a Create new subflow button. Creating one mints a workflow named Subflow followed by a short identifier, containing a Start node wired to an End node, saves it, publishes it and links it to the node in one step. That is the quickest way to start, because a child that has never been saved cannot be resolved and produces a not-found error. If

Select its End node to edit Subflow outputs (to caller) — the local variables it produces and hands back. Each row is a name and a type, chosen from string, number, boolean and object. While you edit the child, its declared locals appear in the Workflow variables panel so they can be referenced and dragged like any other variable. Until a child declares something, its caller has not

title: Binding on the caller
text: The Sub-flow node card shows two folders, Inputs (global → local) and Outputs (local → global), with one slot per declared local of the child. Each slot can be filled in two ways: drag a variable pill from the Workflow variables panel onto it, or type directly into the inline field. An input slot accepts either a bound variable or a literal value or expression. An output slot takes the name of a caller variable to write the result into; when that name is not one the caller already knows, the slot is tagged NEW so it is obvious you are creating a variable rather than filling an existing one. text: Data does not travel through the ports. It travels through variables, and the two maps you fill in are the only bridge. Only the declared maps cross. Everything else in the child is namespaced away. Every call site gets its own prefix, so calling the same sub-flow twice in one workflow — or nesting it — cannot make the two invocations trample each other's variables. Any Set Variable or Set Variables node inside the child has its target name rewritten with that prefix at compile time. If the node has no target chosen yet, the status bar says Pick a workflow for this subflow before opening it. title: Grouping is not a sub-flow
text: The Group button next to Extract does something entirely different. A group is a coloured frame drawn around two or more selected nodes: an editor-only annotation that can be labelled, tinted, collapsed to a chip and moved as a unit. It changes nothing about execution — the nodes inside it run exactly as they did before, keep their own wires, and are compiled individually. Use a group when a stretch of a large graph needs a name so it can be read. Use a sub-flow when the same steps are needed in more than one place, or when the graph is genuinely too big for one canvas. Group membership and th

title: Diagnostics
text: The diagnostics panel in the bottom-left corner of the canvas is the editor's report on whether the graph you have drawn can actually be compiled. This page lists every check that exists, which of them stop you publishing and which merely warn, how to jump from a message to the node or wire that caused it, and — just as usefully — which plausible-sounding checks do not exist, so you do not go looking for warnings that will never appear.

title: Where the messages come from
text: There is no rule engine in the browser. Every message you see is produced by the backend compiler and sent to the editor, which only presents and navigates them. That matters because it means the editor and the publish step agree by construction: what the panel shows is what publishing will decide. Two streams feed the panel: A live pass runs about half a second after the graph stops changing. It compiles the current canvas without saving anything and returns every diagnostic, including non-blocking ones. It is keyed to the graph's meaningful shape, so moving a node or changing the selection d

title: Reading the panel
text: The panel renders nothing when there is nothing to report — an empty corner means a clean graph. When it does appear, its header summarises the counts by severity, colour-coded red for errors, amber for warnings and blue for information, and the whole panel is bordered in the colour of the worst thing in it. Clicking the header collapses it to that summary bar, so it never has to be in your way. Each row shows the diagnostic's code in brackets, its message, and where it applies — either · edge or · node followed by the node id. Clicking a row centres the canvas on the offending element and sel

title: Errors and warnings
text: Severity is what decides everything. Only Error blocks. A warning never prevents a save, a publish or a run — it rides along with the successful response and stays visible in the panel. The severity model also has an Info level, but the compiler never produces one, so in practice you will only ever see errors and warnings.

It has exactly two rules and returns nothing at all when the graph has no device block: Code Severity Message DEVICE_NO_TARGET Error Device block has wired pins but no target selected — its rules cannot run. Pick a target. DEAD_END_WIRE Warning An event is wired but its path reaches nothing that runs — the wire does nothing. title: What actually blocks Save & Publish
text: Publishing runs four gates in order, and stops at the first that fails. Only the last of them produces the compilation diagnostics described above; the first three are separate checks with their own messages. Publishing stops at the first failing gate. Saving the draft is a separate, earlier step. Unbound credential slots. A workflow inserted from a template can carry placeholder credential references. title: Save, publish, run — which are gated
text: Action Gated by Saving the workflow definition Compilation errors only. Saving a draft version Nothing. Work in progress always saves. Publishing · activating a version All four gates. Triggering a run Compilation errors. Importing a workflow Nothing. Diagnostics come back as warnings and the imported version is left inactive. In the editor, the Save & Publish button turns amber and counts the blocking errors — Save & Publish (2 errors) — but stays clickable, because pressing it still saves your draft. Only the publish half will be refused.

title: Checks that do not exist
text: It is worth being explicit about this, because these are the warnings people expect from a graph editor and then quietly assume are passing: There is no orphan-node check . A node connected to nothing publishes cleanly and simply never runs. There is no reachability analysis . A branch that can never be entered is not reported. There is no duplicate-id check . Expressions are never validated . A reference to a node that does not exist publishes without complaint and resolves to nothing at run time, as described in Expressions and data . title: Runtime arming
text: Arming is the one switch that separates design time from run time. While the runtime is disarmed, nothing starts a workflow except you; while it is armed, schedules, webhooks, polls and inbound device signals are all live. It is a single global switch — there is no per-workflow arming — and it is deliberately sticky: several things turn it off automatically, but nothing ever turns it back on for you.

title: Where the switch lives
text: The control is the pill button in the application header, to the right of the navigation. It has exactly three appearances: Armed in green with a filled shield while automatic execution is enabled, Disarmed in amber with a crossed-out shield while it is paused, and a muted Runtime… label during the brief moment after page load when the current state has not arrived from the server yet. The button is disabled while it is loading and while a change is in flight, so a double click cannot leave the interface and the server disagreeing. Changing the switch is an administrator action. It is the mast

title: What arming actually gates
text: Automatic execution requires two independent conditions to be true, and it is worth being precise about which is which. The runtime must be armed, and the individual workflow must be enabled. Disabling a single workflow does not disarm the instance, and disarming the instance does not disable any workflow — they are separate switches that both have to allow a run through. Every automatic start path consults the switch: Start path Behaviour while disarmed Cron scheduler The scheduling loop still ticks every ten seconds but skips schedule evaluation entirely. Nothing is queued and no schedule is

title: The state is stored in the database
text: When you flip the switch, the new value is written to the application settings table under the key that records runtime arming. On the next start-up — after the schema migration and before any worker begins evaluating anything — that stored value is read back and applied. An instance you armed once stays armed across restarts, upgrades and service recycles. The precedence is worth memorising, because it explains almost every "why is my configuration being ignored" question about this setting: The persisted value , if one has ever been written by the switch. Otherwise the configuration seed Run

title: Opening the editor disarms the runtime
text: Navigating into the canvas editor automatically disarms the instance. The rule is precisely "on entering the editor from any other screen" — moving between workflows inside the editor does not re-trigger it, and leaving the editor does not undo it. Re-arming is always a deliberate, manual click on the header switch. This is the behaviour that surprises people most, so it is worth stating its two consequences plainly. First, the automatic disarm goes through the same endpoint as a manual one, so it is persisted . If you open a workflow to read it, close the browser and never touch the switch, t

title: The low-disk guard disarms and stays disarmed
text: A background guard samples free space on the volume holding the data directory. When free space falls below the floor, it disarms the runtime so that no new automatic run starts, and it logs at critical level: every run writes many journal rows, and a database that runs out of room mid-write is a much worse failure than a paused schedule. The policy is read live from Settings › Retention on every check, so changing it applies from the next tick without a restart. Where nothing has been stored there, the configuration section supplies the fallback: Setting Default Effect Storage__MinFreeSpaceMb

title: Other things that read the switch
text: Restoring a backup is refused while the runtime is armed. The restore replaces all current state, so it insists that nothing can be firing mid-restore; the restore panel makes disarming the first of its guided steps and blocks the confirmation until the switch reads Disarmed . This is checked before any decryption or write, so a refused restore leaves the existing data untouched.

title: Reading the state without the interface
text: The current value is exposed as a plain read for monitoring. A one-field JSON response with an armed boolean is what the header pill itself renders, and it is the honest answer to "is this instance live?" — far more reliable than inferring it from whether runs are appearing.

title: Troubleshooting
text: Symptom Likely cause Manual runs work, scheduled runs do not. Disarmed. Manual paths bypass the switch entirely, which is exactly what makes this symptom diagnostic. A webhook caller gets HTTP 409 mentioning the runtime. Disarmed. A 409 that mentions deactivation or a missing active version is a different problem — the workflow is disabled or has never been published and activated. The instance disarms itself repeatedly. Either the low-disk guard is tripping — check the logs for the critical free-space message — or somebody is opening the editor. It came up disarmed despite Runtime__Armed=true

title: Triggers
text: A run begins in exactly one of six ways: you press Run, an HTTP caller posts to the webhook endpoint, a cron schedule comes due, a polling trigger sees something new, another workflow fails and hands off to the error workflow, or an external device raises a signal. This page covers each of them — what configures it, what it produces, and how it fails.

title: Triggers run the active version, not your draft

A run always executes an immutable published version — specifically the one currently marked active — never the working draft in your editor. The webhook, scheduler, polling and simulate-signal endpoints all resolve the active version and refuse with HTTP 409 and the message "Workflow has no active version. Publish and activate a version before triggering execution." when there is not one. The editor's Run button is not an exception; it is the mechanism that makes t

title: Manual runs

The button is disabled until at least one version has been published — its tooltip then reads "Publish a version (Save & Publish) before running." Running while previewing an older version is allowed: the preview closes and the previewed version is what runs. The run's origin is recorded as manual . Starting a run does not navigate away from the editor; a non-disruptive toast reports that the run started, and the graph's variable pins and per-node status colours fill in live while you keep w

title: Cron schedules
text: A Cron Scheduler node carries a five-field cron expression and an IANA time-zone identifier. The property form offers two modes. Simple builds the expression from a frequency (every N minutes, hourly, daily, weekdays, weekly, monthly) plus the day and time controls that frequency needs, and shows the generated expression underneath so you can see what it produced. Advanced (cron) exposes the raw expression: five fields in the order minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week , with Sunday as 0 , * for any, */5 for steps and 1-5 for ranges. An expression the simple builder cannot represent opens

title: Polling triggers
text: A polling trigger asks a source whether anything has changed and starts a run only when the answer is yes. Three fields are always present. Source Kind http · openapi Whether to call a URL directly or an operation from an imported OpenAPI specification. Required. title: The Error Trigger
text: An Error Trigger node marks a workflow as the entry point of an error handler. It takes no configuration: which workflow plays that role is a single global choice made in Settings › Notifications . When any other workflow fails, the chosen workflow is started with the origin error , and the failure context — the failed workflow, run, node, node type, message, original trigger origin and timestamp — is emitted on the node's result port and also flattened into individual global variables. The handler is never re-triggered by its own failures. This is covered in full on the error-handling page.

title: External device signals
text: A graph containing External Device blocks reacts to signals from a connected system: device events the device raises, and incoming actions it sends. Each wired output pin becomes an entry point, and when a matching signal arrives the engine starts an ordinary run seeded at that pin's downstream nodes. Inbound signals are gated by the arming switch. While disarmed the subscription stays connected and the signal is simply dropped, so nothing has to be re-registered when you arm the instance again. Duplicate deliveries of the same signal instance — a provider re-sending a still-active event after

title: Manual Run is disabled for these graphs
text: When a graph contains an External Device block and has no Start or Manual Trigger node, the toolbar hides the Run button. In its place sits a non-interactive emerald status badge reading Event-driven · runs on device events . It is a status, not a disabled button: there is nothing for a manual run to start, because the device block itself is inert and a generic run would execute it as a disconnected no-op and never flow out of the pin. Two real actions sit next to that badge. Watch live runs → opens the run inspector on this workflow's most recent run and then follows new device-event runs as

title: The Simulate signal dialog

Choosing an action reveals a Sample fields section with one input per statically known field of that action; blank fields are omitted from the payload, and an action with no static fields says so and sends an empty payload. Choosing an event says instead that it fires the event as "started" with an empty payload. Fire signal starts the run and opens it in the run inspector immediately — unlike a background Run, a simulation is an explicit test, so it takes

title: Firing a schedule by hand
text: The run inspector's Schedule Controls panel lists every scheduler node in the workflow with its next fire time, its cron expression and time zone, and a Fire now button. Firing by hand starts a run immediately without disturbing the schedule's own next occurrence. It requires the workflow to be enabled and to have an active version, and it refuses with 400 if the node named is not a scheduler node. The resulting run is recorded with the origin schedule , so it appears alongside genuinely scheduled runs in the history.

title: Runs and the inspector
text: The Execution Visualizer is where a run stops being an abstraction. It shows the same graph you drew, coloured by what actually happened, beside a timeline of every journal entry the run produced — and it lets you step backwards through the run, re-run it from any node, and act on nodes that stopped and asked for a decision. It is the debugger, not just a log viewer.

title: Opening a run
section: Running and debugging · Runs and the inspector
text: The visualizer opens from several places: the Execution Visualizer entry in the header once a run is selected, a run in the dashboard history, the Dead Letter list, or automatically when you fire a device signal from the editor. The screen is split: the graph fills the left, and a resizable sidebar on the right carries the run's state and timeline. Drag the divider to widen the sidebar; the width is remembered. The header above the graph shows the workflow name, a shortened run identifier, the run's status, and — when this run is a replay — a pill naming the source run and the node it resumed

The canvas is pan-and-zoom with the usual controls in the bottom-right, and it frames the whole graph once the nodes have been measured, so a run opens showing everything rather than a corner of it. Nodes can be dragged out of the way for legibility, but nothing here edits the workflow: wiring is disabled, and position changes are not saved. The visualizer subscribes to the run's event stream and reacts to workflow start, node start, node completion, node failure, node resumption, suspension, and workflow completion or failure. Each event appends its journal entry to the timeline and advances the corresponding node's colour; the full run state is then refetched so the variables panel and per-node inputs and outputs stay in step. text: The top panel lists the run's global variables and their current values, or reports that no state variables have been mutated yet. Values that look like secrets are masked before the run is handed to the browser; the full value stays in the database for replay and debugging, but a runtime-fetched token is never rendered here.

title: Schedule Controls

Each card has a Fire now button that starts a run immediately without disturbing the schedule's own next occurrence. A workflow with no scheduler nodes says so.

title: Manual Actions
section: Running and debugging · Runs and the inspector
text: When a node is stopped awaiting a decision, a red-tinted panel appears above the timeline listing each such node with the reason. See Manual decisions below.

section: Running and debugging · Runs and the inspector
text: The timeline is the heart of the sidebar. Its header counts the nodes and the total elapsed time and carries the run's overall status. Directly beneath it, a coloured banner names the trigger: cyan AUTO for a schedule, with the cron expression and next fire time; emerald EVENT or ACTION for a device signal; violet MANUAL otherwise. Each executed node is one group in the timeline, connected by a vertical rail whose colour follows the status of the steps on either side. A collapsed group shows its title, its status chip, the wall-clock time it started, the offset from the start of the run, and a

title: Child runs
section: Running and debugging · Runs and the inspector
text: Some nodes start runs of their own, and the timeline links to them rather than inlining them. An AI Agent group renders its per-iteration tool-call trail — each turn, each call, whether it succeeded, and the short identifier of the child run it produced. A failed run that was caught by the global error workflow gains a link to the handler run, both inside the failed group and as a button under the timeline.

title: Hiding skipped branches
section: Running and debugging · Runs and the inspector
text: A device-event run fans out across every wired pin, but only one of them fires; the rest appear as skipped noise. On those runs the timeline hides skipped groups by default and offers a Show N skipped branches toggle at the bottom of the list. The filter is scoped to device-event runs on purpose — a meaningful skip elsewhere, such as an operator's Skip decision or a condition's untaken branch, always stays visible.

title: The Time Travel inspector
section: Running and debugging · Runs and the inspector
text: Step Through in the header opens a panel across the bottom of the graph that walks the run one node at a time, in execution order. A run that is already finished when you open it starts in step mode automatically, positioned on the first failed step when there is one; a run that is still in progress stays in the live view, and once you toggle the mode by hand your choice sticks for that run. The panel header carries previous and next buttons with a Step n / total counter, the node's title and status, the time it started, how long it ran, and its offset from the start of the run. title: Replaying from a node

text: Right-click any node on the graph to open the Re-run from here dialog. A replay creates a brand-new run that inherits the source run's upstream node states — their historical inputs and outputs are reused as-is — and re-executes the node you picked together with everything downstream of it. The variables it starts from are the exact snapshot taken when that node originally began. The source run is never modified. The dialog offers two choices: Target version. Defaults to This run's version (original) , so a replay reproduces the original conditions. Any published version can be selected instea

title: Manual decisions
section: Running and debugging · Runs and the inspector
text: A node can end up in a state where the engine refuses to guess. The usual cause is a crash or restart in the middle of a non-idempotent side effect: the journal records that the effect was attempted but never records its completion, so on recovery the engine cannot know whether the payment went out. Rather than risk a duplicate, it parks the node with the message "Execution interrupted during a non-idempotent side effect. Manual decision required." and suspends the run. When the visualizer recognises one — the error says the file access was denied and names the attempted path — it renders an amber How to fix card immediately after the failure, so the reading order is cause then cure.
