title: Versions and publishing
text: Three things share a name in casual conversation and must not be confused: the draft you are editing, the published versions that have been frozen from it, and the one version that is currently active and therefore actually runs. Almost every "my change did not take effect" report is a mismatch between those three, and this page is about keeping them straight.

title: The three states
section: Running and debugging · Versions and publishing
text: State What it is Can it run? Draft The mutable graph in the canvas editor. One per workflow. Autosaves as you work. Never directly. Published version An immutable snapshot of the nodes and edges, numbered and dated, kept forever unless retention prunes it. Only once activated. Active version The single published version currently designated live. Recorded in an append-only activation log. Yes — this is what every trigger executes. Publishing freezes a version; activating chooses which frozen version runs. Nothing is ever overwritten.

title: Publishing
section: Running and debugging · Versions and publishing
text: Save & Publish in the canvas toolbar freezes the current draft into a new, numbered, immutable version. The button reports what it will do: it reads Saved when there is nothing new to publish, and when the graph has blocking diagnostics it turns amber and counts them, so you cannot publish a broken graph without noticing. Publishing runs a compile and a runnability gate before writing anything. Three conditions block it outright, each with an explicit message rather than a cryptic runtime failure later: Unbound credential slots. The version references a credential placeholder that is not bound

title: Activation
section: Running and debugging · Versions and publishing
text: Publishing alone changes nothing about what runs. Activation is the separate act of designating one published version as live, and it is recorded in an append-only activation log with who did it, when, why, which version was active before, and — for a restore — which version it was copied from. That log is what lets the instance answer "what was live at 3 a.m. last Tuesday?" after the fact. There are three ways to activate a version: Pressing Run in the editor. Run activates the version selected in the toolbar dropdown and then triggers it, every time, so the selection is always what executes.

title: The runtime-version dropdown
section: Running and debugging · Versions and publishing
text: The toolbar's version control is a custom list rather than a plain dropdown, because the states it needs to show cannot be expressed by one. Its trigger button shows the selected version number and whether it is ACTIVE or merely being VIEWING ed. Inside, each row shows the version number, a relative timestamp, a dot indicating whether it has ever produced runs, and a badge marking the Active version or, failing that, the Latest one. The hint at the top of the list names the two distinct actions, because conflating them is the classic mistake: clicking a row previews the version read-only and i

title: Version history
section: Running and debugging · Versions and publishing
text: Ctrl + Shift + H — Cmd + Shift + H on a Mac — opens the version-history drawer on the right edge of the editor. It fetches only while it is open, so it costs nothing in the background, and it lists metadata rather than whole graphs. Each row shows the version number, an ACTIVE badge where applicable, the origin badge, the label if one was given, the creation timestamp and author, the node count, and the number of runs that version has produced. Clicking a row opens a read-only preview; hovering it for a moment does the same automatically. A Diff button on each row compares that version directl

title: Read-only preview
section: Running and debugging · Versions and publishing
text: Previewing a version renders it on the canvas behind a sticky banner reading Previewing version N with a READ-ONLY tag. Editing, autosave and publishing are all disabled while it is up; the live draft is untouched behind it and is never mutated by anything you do in preview. The banner carries the actions that belong to the mode. Diff compares this version against the working draft. Restore this version makes it the current, live one — hidden when you are already previewing the active version, since there would be nothing to restore. Exit preview , or Esc , returns to the draft. The banner's s

title: Diffing
section: Running and debugging · Versions and publishing
text: The diff panel opens on the right and is titled with its two sides — for example active v3 → working draft . It is computed in the browser from the two payloads, using the same mapper that save and publish use, so the comparison is genuinely apples to apples.

title: Behavioural changes versus cosmetic ones
section: Running and debugging · Versions and publishing
text: The diff enforces one hard rule: behavioural changes are shown, cosmetic layout changes are collapsed . A node that was only moved or resized is not a change to what the workflow does, and letting a tidy-up session drown out one edited field makes the diff useless. Behavioural changes are nodes added or removed, a node's type changing, any configuration field changing, and connections added or removed. These are listed immediately, each with an added , removed or changed badge, the node identifier, and for a changed node the individual field paths with their before and after values struck thro

title: Restoring an old version
section: Running and debugging · Versions and publishing
text: Restore is fork-forward , not rewind. It copies the chosen version's graph into a brand-new version at the top of the history and makes that copy live. Nothing is overwritten and no version is deleted — the history stays append-only, and the version you restored from remains exactly where it was. The confirmation dialog states this plainly and adds the warning that matters most: a restore affects future executions only . It does not undo side effects already caused by runs of the newer version. Mail that was sent stays sent; rows that were written stay written. Restoring is a way to change wha

title: How many versions are kept
section: Running and debugging · Versions and publishing
text: By default, all of them. Retention__MaxWorkflowVersionsPerWorkflow defaults to 0 , which disables the cap; the setting is also editable at Settings › Retention , and the stored value wins over the configuration file. Setting it to a positive number lets the retention sweep keep the newest N versions per workflow and delete older ones. The cap is deliberately not absolute. Three classes of version are preserved no matter how far past the limit they fall: The active version of every workflow. Anything referenced by the activation log — including the version a restore was copied from and the vers

title: Error handling and alerts
text: A failure can be handled at three levels, and they compose rather than compete: the node itself can retry, the graph can route the failure down an error port, and the instance can start a dedicated error workflow and notify you. This page covers what happens at each level, in the order the engine tries them.

title: What happens when a node fails
section: Running and debugging · Error handling and alerts
text: When a node throws, the engine works through a fixed sequence: Automatic retry, if the node opts in. A node whose catalog entry declares the retry recovery mode and an idempotent side-effect kind is retried according to its retry policy. The run parks in a waiting-for-retry state and a delayed work item is enqueued per the backoff. Both conditions are required — a node that causes a non-idempotent side effect is never retried automatically, because repeating it is not safe. An error port, if one is wired. Once retries are exhausted or not applicable, the engine looks for outgoing edges from th

title: Per-node error ports
section: Running and debugging · Error handling and alerts
text: An error port is just an output socket named error or failure , and the engine treats both names identically and case-insensitively. Nodes that expose one — the Inline Code node, for example, carries result and error — let you wire the failure path on the canvas exactly like the success path. Everything downstream of that edge runs with the failure already in hand. Loop and iteration nodes reserve their own port names, so success , failure and error are all recognised as exit paths out of a loop rather than as part of the loop body. A parallel iteration collects a per-item error into that item

title: The global error workflow
section: Running and debugging · Error handling and alerts
text: One workflow per instance can be nominated as the error handler. It is chosen from the Error Workflow card at Settings › Notifications , a single dropdown listing every workflow with — None (disabled) — as the default. The choice saves immediately and confirms with "Saved." or "Cleared." Whenever any run fails, the failed run's identifier is handed off — as a non-blocking in-memory hand-off, so it can never slow down or break the run that failed — to a background worker that starts the error workflow. Every path that marks a run failed flows through the same chokepoint, so there is no category

title: Loop prevention
section: Running and debugging · Error handling and alerts
text: Two guards stop an error handler from triggering itself, and both must pass before a handler run is started: The failed workflow is not itself the configured error workflow. The failed run was not itself started as an error handler — that is, its origin is not error . The second guard is the one that matters in practice: it means a handler that fails while handling someone else's failure does not spawn another handler. When either guard blocks the dispatch it is logged at debug level and nothing else happens — so a broken error workflow fails silently as far as the interface is concerned, whic

title: What the handler receives
section: Running and debugging · Error handling and alerts
text: The handler is started with the origin error and a link back to the run it is handling. The failure context arrives twice, in two shapes, so you can use whichever suits the node you are wiring. As a bundled object on the Error Trigger node's result port: Field Contains workflowId Identifier of the workflow that failed. workflowName Its display name. executionId Identifier of the failed run. failedNodeId The node that failed. failedNodeType That node's type, resolved from the failed workflow's definition. errorMessage The failure message. triggerOrigin How the failed run had been started. times

title: Failure-alert channels
section: Running and debugging · Error handling and alerts
text: Alerts are separate from the error workflow and fire from the same run-failed event. Destinations are managed as Notification Channels at Settings › Notifications . Each channel has a name, a type, and type-specific configuration. Type Configuration Webhook (generic JSON POST) A single Webhook URL . The failure message is posted to it as JSON. Slack (incoming webhook) A Slack Incoming Webhook URL of the usual hooks.slack.com/services/… form. E-Mail (SMTP) SMTP Host , Port (default 587), a Use SSL/TLS switch (on by default), Username and Password , a From Address — which falls back to the usern

title: Test send
section: Running and debugging · Error handling and alerts
text: Every channel card has a Test button that sends a message through the real sender with the real stored configuration. The result appears on the card itself: Sending… , then ✓ Test sent or ✗ followed by the actual error. This is the only way to find out that an SMTP password is wrong or a Slack webhook has been revoked before a genuine failure needs it, and it costs nothing — use it after every edit.

title: Which channels a workflow alerts
section: Running and debugging · Error handling and alerts
text: Routing is per workflow, chosen from the alerts chip on the workflow's card in the dashboard. There are three modes, and the resolution is deliberately simple: Mode Chip reads Resolves to Default channels (Inherit) Alerts: Default, green Every channel marked as a default failure-alert channel. This is the mode a workflow has until you change it. Off Alerts: Off, red No channels. This workflow never alerts. Custom channels Alerts: Custom, violet Exactly the channels you tick, ignoring the default flag entirely. A channel is marked as a default with the Use as default failure-alert channel check

title: Delivery and its failures
section: Running and debugging · Error handling and alerts
text: Alerting can never affect a workflow run. Dispatch happens on a background worker, and every send is wrapped so a delivery failure is recorded but never propagates back into execution. Each channel's outcome is journaled onto the failed run itself, with the channel's identifier, name and type attached — so the run timeline of a failure also tells you whether the alert about it went out, and to where. A send that throws is journaled as a notification failure with the exception message. That is where to look first when someone says the alert never arrived: if there is no notification entry at al

title: Navigating between a failure and its handler
section: Running and debugging · Error handling and alerts
text: A failed run and the handler run it spawned are linked in both directions, and the visualizer makes both directions one click. A pill floats at the top-centre of the run canvas. On a failed run it is a solid amber Error handler ran → button that opens the handler. On the handler run it is a coral-outlined Triggered by failed run → button that navigates back to the failure. When a run is both — a handler that itself failed and was handled — both pills appear side by side. There are three further entry points to the same handler run, so it is discoverable wherever you happen to be reading: A syn

title: Putting the layers together
section: Running and debugging · Error handling and alerts
text: A sensible default arrangement for a production instance is all four layers at once. Let idempotent nodes retry themselves. Wire an error port only where the graph genuinely has a fallback, and deliberately leave it unwired where it does not, so the run fails and the rest of the machinery engages. Configure one default notification channel and test it, so a human hears about it. Nominate one error workflow — published, activated and tested — so the failure gets recorded or escalated consistently regardless of which workflow produced it. What is left over lands in the dead letter queue for tria

title: Dead letter queue
text: The dead letter queue is the instance's inbox of failed runs. It is not a separate store and nothing is moved into it — it is a filtered view of the runs whose status is Failed, kept as a distinct screen so that "things that broke and nobody has looked at yet" is a list you can drive to zero rather than a status you have to remember to filter for.

title: Where it is
section: Running and debugging · Dead letter queue
text: Dead Letter is a top-level entry in the header navigation. The screen is a single column: a heading, a Refresh button, one row per failed run, and a line of explanatory text. When there is nothing to triage it says "No failed runs. 🎉" — which is the state you are aiming for. The list does not update by itself. It loads when you open the screen and reloads when you press Refresh, so a run that fails while you are looking at the list will not appear until you ask for it.

title: What lands here
section: Running and debugging · Dead letter queue
text: Exactly the runs whose status is Failed . In practice that means a node failed and nothing in the graph caught it : automatic retries were exhausted or did not apply, and no outgoing edge named error or failure was wired from the failed node. It also includes runs an operator failed deliberately with the Fail Run decision on a node awaiting a manual decision. Just as important is what does not land here: Not listed Why Runs that caught their own failure on an error port Following an error edge lets the run continue, so it never reaches Failed status. Cancelled runs Cancelled is its own status

title: Reading a row
section: Running and debugging · Dead letter queue
text: Each row shows the workflow's name — falling back to its identifier when the name is unavailable — and, underneath, the run's trigger origin and the time it last changed, formatted for your locale. The origin is the useful half: a wall of schedule rows says something systemic broke, whereas a single webhook row among them points at one caller. The row itself carries no error message. That is deliberate — a failure message is frequently a multi-line dump, and the list is a triage queue, not a log. The message lives one click away.

title: Triage: open or discard
section: Running and debugging · Dead letter queue
text: Every row has exactly two actions, which is the whole workflow of the screen.

title: Open
section: Running and debugging · Dead letter queue
text: Open loads the run in the Execution Visualizer, which is where all the actual diagnosis happens: the failed node highlighted on the graph it ran against, the expanded failure group in the timeline with the full error, the Time Travel inspector for the inputs and variables as they stood at each step, and right-click replay to re-run from any node — optionally against a newer version, which is how you verify a fix against the exact run that exposed the bug. A replay creates a new run and never modifies the source. The original therefore stays in the dead letter list until you discard it, which i

title: Discard
section: Running and debugging · Dead letter queue
text: Discard marks the run as Discarded so it drops off the list, and writes an ExecutionDiscarded journal entry recording that it was discarded from the dead-letter view. Only a failed run can be discarded — anything else is refused with the message "Only failed executions can be discarded." Discarding is not a delete and not a retry. It changes a status and nothing else: The run, its journal, its per-node states and its inputs and outputs all remain in the database and remain openable if you have the run's identifier. Nothing is re-executed and nothing is compensated. Whatever the run did before

title: How it relates to the error workflow
section: Running and debugging · Dead letter queue
text: The dead letter queue and the global error workflow react to the same event — a run reaching Failed status — but they are complementary rather than alternatives, and neither suppresses the other. Error workflow Failure alerts Dead letter queue When Immediately, in the background Immediately, in the background When you next open the screen Who acts A workflow you wrote A channel you configured A person Good for Automatic compensation, escalation, ticket creation Telling somebody Deciding what actually happened Clears itself n/a n/a Only when you discard A failed run therefore does three things

title: The list empties itself eventually
section: Running and debugging · Dead letter queue
text: Retention prunes terminal runs older than Retention__RunHistoryDays , which defaults to 30 days, and deleting a run cascades to its journal and node states. Failed runs are terminal, so an untriaged failure disappears from this list once it ages out — along with the evidence needed to diagnose it. That is the argument for keeping the queue near zero rather than treating it as an archive. If you need failures to persist longer than they are being investigated, raise the retention window at Settings › Retention ; note that a stored value there overrides the configuration file, and that keeping e

title: How to read this reference
text: Every node in the reference is documented the same way: what it does, its parameters with types, and its output ports. This page explains what those columns mean — where a node's identity comes from, why the palette group rarely matches the category in the catalog, which fields accept expressions, and why a property form is blank even when the code behind it has a sensible default. Read it once; the six pages that follow assume it.

title: Where a node's facts come from
section: Node reference · How to read this reference
text: A node is described by a manifest : a small record holding its id, display name, category, parameters, output ports, capability tags, timeout and retry policy. The built-in manifests are registered in code when the application starts. The property form, the palette entry, the ports drawn on the canvas and the compiler's socket validation are all generated from that one record, which is why an entry in this reference can be trusted to match what you see on screen. What the manifest does not describe is behaviour. The value a node emits, the shape of its payload and every fallback it applies to

title: Display name and internal id
section: Node reference · How to read this reference
text: Each entry's heading is the display name — what the palette, the canvas and the properties panel call it. Immediately after it, in monospace, is the internal id : the string stored in the workflow file, quoted in compiler diagnostics and journal entries, and used by the REST API. They frequently disagree, and the id is the one that matters when you are reading an error message. Cron Scheduler is stored as scheduler ; Email Send (SMTP) is smtpSend ; Parallel For-Each is parallelForEach . Ids are matched case-insensitively throughout the engine, but they are written in the workflow exactly as th

title: Palette category
section: Node reference · How to read this reference
text: The category in the manifest is not the group you see in the sidebar. The palette normalises nine manifest categories down to six sections, and the collapsing is lossy: Utility , Scripting , Annotations , External and anything it does not recognise all land in a single Utility section. This is why Inline Code — category Scripting in the catalog — appears under Utility in the palette. Manifest category Palette section Triggers Trigger Control Logic Data Data Integrations Network AI Ai Utility Utility Scripting Utility Annotations Utility (but hidden — see below) External Utility anything else U

title: Parameters
section: Node reference · How to read this reference
text: A parameter is configuration you fill in on the node; it is not the same thing as data arriving over a wire. Every parameter carries a name, a type, and a required flag. The Required column in this reference reflects the manifest's own flag — the publish gate uses it to refuse a workflow with an unconfigured required field, so a missing required value fails at publish time rather than mid-run. Type Field rendered Notes string Single-line text, or a resizable text area Switches to a multi-line editor automatically for long or multi-line values, and always for fields such as body , message , pro

title: Which parameters accept expressions
section: Node reference · How to read this reference
text: Each parameter carries an expression flag, listed in the Expr column of every parameter table. When it is set, the engine resolves {{ }} placeholders in the value before handing it to the node: # an upstream node's output {{ $node.httpRequest-1.output.body }} # a workflow variable, including a nested path {{ $variables.customer.email }} {{ $variables.rows[0].id }} When the flag is clear, the raw value is handed over untouched. That is not an oversight — it is load-bearing. Inline Code's code parameter must not be rewritten, or a {{ }} sequence inside a C# string literal would be mangled before

title: Output ports
section: Node reference · How to read this reference
text: Ports are the sockets on the right edge of a node card. The manifest declares them, the canvas draws one handle per declared port, and the compiler checks that every edge names a port that exists. Three shapes occur. Single, branch and dynamic ports. Only declared ports are socket-validated. A single result port is the common case: the node did its work and the run continues. Branch ports mean the node chooses one wire. Condition emits on true or false ; HTTP Request on success or error ; container nodes on start for each pass through the body and success once the loop is done. Only the chosen

title: Capabilities and what "privileged" means
section: Node reference · How to read this reference
text: A manifest lists the privileged resources its node touches as capability tags. Five of them are classed as privileged , meaning a workflow containing such a node can reach past ordinary data flow and touch the host itself. That classification is what drives the warning shown before you install an imported template or bundle, and before you accept an AI-generated graph. Tag Privileged Enforcement filesystem.read Privileged Checked against the file access policy on every call. Deny-all until directories are permitted. filesystem.write Privileged Same policy, separate permission. code.execute Pri

title: Credentials
section: Node reference · How to read this reference
text: Any parameter typed credentialRef stores nothing but the id of a credential saved under Settings › Credentials . The secret is decrypted and injected at run time. This is why exporting a workflow never leaks a password, and equally why importing one onto a different instance leaves the credential reference dangling until you point it at a local credential.

title: Timeouts
section: Node reference · How to read this reference
text: Every manifest carries a default timeout in seconds, listed in each node entry. The engine starts from that value and applies two adjustments: A timeoutSeconds (or timeout ) property on the node overrides it, clamped to between 1 and 3600 seconds. A manifest timeout of 0 means "not specified"; a node that actually executes then gets a 5-second timeout. Most nodes declaring 0 are triggers, which never execute a task at all, so the fallback rarely bites. Delay is special-cased: its timeout is raised to the configured wait plus two seconds, so a long deliberate pause can never trip a limit that e

title: Retry behaviour
section: Node reference · How to read this reference
text: A node is retried automatically only when both manifest flags allow it: its recovery mode must be "retry automatically" and its side effect must be idempotent. Declaring only the first is not enough, and that combination is easy to misread. HTTP Request asks for automatic retry but is marked as having a non-idempotent side effect, so a failed HTTP Request is never retried by the engine — a POST that may have already been delivered must not be replayed on the run's behalf. The same applies to Database Query, Email Send and MQTT Publish. The nodes that genuinely retry are File Read, Email Fetch

title: Trigger nodes
text: A trigger is where a run begins. Which trigger fires is decided by the run's origin — manual, schedule, webhook, poll or error — matched against the trigger nodes the workflow actually contains. This page documents all seven nodes in the Triggers category, including End , which is filed here despite being a terminator rather than a starter.

title: How a trigger is chosen
text: Trigger nodes are marked trigger-only in the catalog, and most of them have no executor at all. When the run reaches one of those, the engine marks it complete immediately and fills its output port with a payload synthesised from the run itself — the schedule's fire time, the polled document, the failure context. Cron Scheduler, Webhook Trigger, Polling Trigger, Error Trigger and Manual Trigger all work this way, which is why their timeout is 0 and why none of them can fail. Start is the exception: it is trigger-only but does have an executor, because it has real work to do at a subflow bounda

title: Start
text: start · Triggers · trigger-only · timeout 0 The default entry point, and the node every new workflow is created with. Reach for it whenever a workflow is run by hand, tested from the editor, called as a subflow, or invoked by an AI Agent as a tool. It is also the fallback entry point for any origin the engine does not recognise, which makes it the safest thing to leave on a graph. Start has no parameters of its own, yet it is not inert. When a workflow is used as a subflow , its Start node is where the caller's input bindings land: each declared input is written into a workflow variable before

title: Cron Scheduler
text: scheduler · Triggers · trigger-only · timeout 0 Runs the workflow on a recurring clock. Use it for anything time-driven: a nightly export, a five-minute health probe, a Monday-morning digest. The properties panel gives you a builder with the common shapes — every N minutes, hourly, daily, weekdays, weekly, monthly — and drops to a raw expression field when the cron you have cannot be represented by the builder, so it never silently rewrites an expression you typed yourself. Both parameters are required, and both are validated when the workflow is saved rather than when it fires. The expression

title: Webhook Trigger
text: webhookTrigger · Triggers · trigger-only · timeout 0 Starts a run when an external system posts to the instance. Reach for it when something else owns the timing — a source-control hook, an alerting system, a form back end. The caller posts the workflow id and an optional bag of input variables; those variables become the run's globals and are readable downstream. The endpoint is deliberately machine-facing and does not require a user session, so it is gated by three other things instead. The runtime must be armed. The workflow must be enabled and have an active version. And, if you have confi

title: Polling Trigger
text: pollingTrigger · Triggers · trigger-only · timeout 0 Watches a source you cannot get a webhook out of, and starts a run when it changes. This is the node with the most configuration in the catalog, because it has to cover two kinds of source and five ways of deciding that something is new. Saving the workflow creates one persisted polling trigger per node, carrying the interval, the source configuration and an opaque cursor holding what was last seen. The cursor survives ordinary edits — retitling the node, adjusting headers — but is reset whenever the source's identity changes, meaning any of

title: Choosing a change-detection mode
text: etag and last-modified lean on the server's own validators. They are the cheapest and most accurate options when the source sets those headers correctly — and they detect nothing at all when it does not. hash compares a digest of the response body. It works against any source, at the cost of transferring the whole body every time, and it reports a change whenever any byte moves — including a timestamp the server stamps into every reply. json-cursor tracks a single value inside the response, named by jsonCursorPath . This is the right choice for a feed with a monotonic id or updatedAt , and the

title: Error Trigger
text: errorTrigger · Triggers · trigger-only · timeout 0 The entry point of the global error-handler workflow. Reach for it once, in one workflow, and nominate that workflow as the instance's error handler; from then on any other workflow that fails starts a run of it with the failure context attached. It is the right place to put alerting, ticket creation or a dead-letter write, because it keeps that logic out of every individual workflow. It has no parameters at all. There is nothing to configure because the routing is a global setting rather than a property of the node, and the payload shape is f

title: End
text: end · Triggers · timeout 0 (5 seconds applied at run time) A terminator, filed in the Triggers category alongside Start because the two form the workflow's interface. On an ordinary workflow it is optional — a path that runs out of wired successors simply ends. Reach for it when you want an explicit, readable finish, and reach for it always in a workflow used as a subflow. That is because End is where a subflow's outputs are declared and copied back to the caller. Each declared output names a local variable and the caller-side name to write it to; without an End node a subflow computes results

title: Manual Trigger
text: manualTrigger · Triggers · trigger-only · timeout 0 · Hidden from the palette A manual entry point: no parameters, a single result port, and the same origin matching as Start. It is documented here only so that an older workflow containing one is not mysterious. It remains registered and executable, and such a workflow renders and runs exactly as before — but you cannot add a new one, because Start does the same job and having two manual entry points to choose between helped nobody. The one behavioural difference is that Manual Trigger has no executor, so it emits nothing: where Start passes a

title: Logic nodes
text: The seven nodes that decide what runs, when, and how many times. They share a manifest category — Control — which the palette shows as Logic . Two of them are containers that hold a body subgraph rather than passing work along a wire, and that distinction changes how you draw the graph.

title: Branch ports and container ports
text: Most nodes hand the run to whatever is wired downstream. A branch node instead picks exactly one of its ports and suppresses every edge leaving the others. Only six node types route this way, and three of them are on this page: Condition, For Loop and Parallel For-Each. That restriction is deliberate — a node such as HTTP Request has several data sockets that must all deliver, so routing has to be opt-in rather than triggered by any node that happens to name a port. Container nodes — For Loop and Parallel For-Each — are drawn as a resizable box you drop other nodes into, and they have three wi

title: Condition
text: condition · Control · timeout 10 · branch node The workhorse of branching: evaluate a test and send the run down true or false . Reach for it for anything that is genuinely a yes-or-no question — an HTTP status worth continuing on, a field that must be present, a threshold being crossed. Its properties panel is not a generic form. Selecting a Condition node replaces the parameter fields with a compact summary and an Edit logic launcher that opens a full-screen editor for building the test out of comparators, groups and negations. The four parameters below are what that editor persists; you do

title: The logic parameter
text: logic holds the whole test as a JSON tree — the modern form, and the one the editor writes. It is versioned: a flat version 1 document is accepted and normalised into a version 2 tree in memory, so older workflows keep working without being rewritten on disk. Comparators are named by short operator ids grouped into five families: Family Operators Arity Comparison eq , ne , gt , gte , lt , lte Binary Text contains , ncontains , starts , ends , regex Binary Membership in , nin Binary Existence empty , nempty , exists , nexists Unary Boolean true , false Unary The tree is bounded, and the bounds

title: The legacy operands
text: left , operator and right are the original single-comparison form, retained so a workflow authored before the logic editor still runs untouched. Precedence is strict: a usable logic value always wins ; the legacy operands are consulted only when logic is absent, empty or whitespace. Opening the node in the logic editor and saving migrates it. The legacy vocabulary is seven names — Equal , NotEqual , GreaterThan , LessThan , GreaterThanOrEqual , LessThanOrEqual , Contains — each mapped onto a modern operator id. A name outside that list is treated as corrupt data and fails the node rather than

title: Delay
text: delay · Control · timeout 60 Waits, then continues. Reach for it to pace a loop against a rate-limited API, to leave a remote system time to settle before polling it back, or to stagger a fan-out. Two parameters express the same thing and only one is read. delayMs wins if it is present at all; duration is consulted only when it is absent, and is parsed as a time span such as 00:05:00 . Neither has a default — an empty node waits zero milliseconds and continues immediately. The threshold worth knowing is one second . A wait of 1000 milliseconds or more suspends the run: the engine schedules a t

title: Switch
text: switch · Control · timeout 10 A multi-way branch: compare one value against a list of case labels and take the matching branch, or default when nothing matches. The catalog registers it, the palette offers it and the compiler recognises it. Switch has no executor in this build No task implementation is registered for the switch type, so a run that reaches one fails the node with No task implementation registered for type 'switch'. and hands control to the workflow's error path. The failure is loud and appears in the run journal, but it happens at run time — publishing and validation both pass.

title: For Loop
text: forLoop · Control · timeout 60 · container · branch node Runs a body repeatedly, one pass at a time, in the order the items arrive. Reach for it when the iterations must not overlap — writing rows to a file, calling an API that will not tolerate concurrency, or accumulating into a variable where order matters. When the iterations are independent, Parallel For-Each is faster. Loop state lives in the run's global variables under keys derived from the node's id, and the presence of the count key is what tells the loop it is on a later pass. That is why the end loop-back is a port and not a value

title: Modes
text: mode drives which other fields the properties panel shows, so the form changes as you change it. The manifest declares four values: count — repeat a fixed number of times, taken from count . The body's item is the index. foreach — iterate a collection from collection . A JSON array is parsed as one; a value that will not parse is split on commas and each piece trimmed, which makes a plain comma-separated string work without ceremony. while — advertised as repeating while condition holds. batch — advertised as iterating collection in chunks of batchSize . Only count and foreach are implemented

title: Parallel For-Each
text: parallelForEach · Control · timeout 300 · container · branch node Runs the same body once per collection item, concurrently. Reach for it when the items are independent and the work is dominated by waiting — enriching a hundred records from an API, fetching a batch of documents, sending a set of notifications. On latency-bound work the difference against For Loop is not marginal. Each item runs in its own in-memory mini-executor with a private copy of the global variables and its own node-state map, so iterations cannot interfere with one another. The consequence is that a body node writing a

title: Bounds and failure
text: maxParallelism defaults to 8 and is clamped to between 1 and 64. continueOnError defaults to false . With it off, one failed item fails the whole node, reporting how many items failed and quoting the first error. With it on, every item is attempted and a failed one contributes an object carrying its error in place of a result — so a partial success is distinguishable from a clean one by inspecting failedCount . Body nodes are timed individually: each body node's manifest timeout is clamped to between 1 and 600 seconds, and a body node declaring no timeout gets 30 seconds rather than the usual

title: Join
text: join · Control · timeout 10 Fan-in. It waits until every branch wired into it has completed, then emits their outputs as a single ordered array. Reach for it after a deliberate fan-out where all branches are guaranteed to run — several independent calls made in parallel, or the branches downstream of a Parallel For-Each. The waiting is done by the engine, not the node: a Join is simply not scheduled until each of its incoming-edge predecessors has completed. By the time the node itself runs, the branch values have already been collected in incoming-edge order, and the node is a thin pass-throu

title: Subflow
text: subflow · Control · timeout 300 Calls another workflow as a step. Reach for it to factor out something you repeat — a notification format, an authentication dance, a validation routine — and to get around the Parallel For-Each restriction on nested control flow, which a subflow satisfies by definition. A subflow is inlined at compile time , not invoked as a separate run. The compiler splices the referenced workflow's nodes and edges into one flat execution plan, prefixing every inlined id with the subflow node's own id — a node called inline-1 inside a subflow node called subflow-a becomes sub

title: Data nodes
text: Three nodes sit in the Data category, and the palette shows them under Data unchanged. Transform pulls one value out of a JSON payload, Merge concatenates two arrays, and Resource Picker turns a design-time choice from a remote system into a value the workflow can rely on. Only Resource Picker touches the network, and only it can fail for reasons outside your graph.

title: Reshaping data without a node
text: Before reaching for a node, remember that most extraction can be done inline. Any parameter whose Expr flag is set accepts {{ }} , and expressions already walk into objects and arrays: {{ $node.httpRequest-1.output.body }} {{ $variables.customer.email }} {{ $variables.rows[0].id }} A Transform node earns its place when the extracted value is used by several downstream nodes, when you want the extraction to appear in the run inspector as its own step, or when a missing value should stop the run rather than quietly resolve to nothing.

title: Transform
text: transform · Data · timeout 10 Takes a JSON document and a path, and emits whatever the path selects. Reach for it to lift a record out of an API response before branching on it, to pull the array out of a paged envelope so a loop can iterate it, or to reduce a large payload to the one field a later node needs. inputJson is expression-enabled, which is how the document gets in — normally a reference to an upstream node's output. If the value arrives as a JSON string it is parsed first; if it is already a structured value it is queried directly. A string that is not valid JSON is treated as a pl

title: The path grammar
text: Despite the parameter name, this is not full JSONPath. It is a deliberately small dotted-path navigator, and knowing its exact shape saves a lot of guessing: Segments are separated by . — data.customer.email . A segment may be followed by [n] to index into an array — items[0] , rows[12] . Indices are whole numbers only. There are no wildcards, filters, slices, recursive descent or string-key brackets. There is no leading $ . Writing $.data.items makes the navigator look for a property literally named $ and find nothing. Every segment must resolve through an object . A path cannot begin by inde

title: Worked examples
text: A paged HTTP response, and the two extractions you almost always want from one — the array to loop over, and a cursor to decide whether to poll again: // inputJson — {{ $node.httpRequest-1.output.body }} { "data" : { "items" : [ { "id" : 4711 , "email" : "ada@example.com" , "state" : "open" }, { "id" : 4712 , "email" : "grace@example.com" , "state" : "closed" } ], "nextCursor" : "eyJwYWdlIjoyfQ" } } // jsonPath: data.items -> the whole array, ready for a For Loop // jsonPath: data.nextCursor -> "eyJwYWdlIjoyfQ" // jsonPath: data.items[0].email-> "ada@example.com" // jsonPath: data.items[9].id

title: Merge
text: merge · Data · timeout 10 Combines two arrays into one. Reach for it after a fan-out where two branches each produced a list and the continuation wants a single collection to iterate — results from two pages, two regions, two systems. Both inputs are expression-enabled strings, which in practice means each holds a reference to an upstream array. Neither is required, so a node with one side wired is accepted rather than rejected. There is no key matching, no de-duplication and no field-level joining: this is concatenation, and two records describing the same entity stay two records. When you ne

title: Resource Picker
text: resourcePicker · Data · timeout 30 · capabilities network , credentials · retried automatically Lets you choose a value from a live list on a remote system while you are editing, and then emits that choice at run time. Reach for it when a workflow needs a specific project, queue, folder or mailbox and you would otherwise paste an opaque identifier into three different nodes and hope it stays correct. Pick it once, promote the result to a workflow variable, and reference the variable everywhere. The value it emits is not a stored copy. At run time the node re-resolves the saved stable key again

title: Network nodes
text: The nodes that reach outside the process — HTTP, SQL, the local filesystem, mail, MQTT, notification channels, and the operations generated from an imported OpenAPI specification. These are the nodes that need a credential, a capability grant, or both, and they are the ones that fail for reasons outside your workflow. Each entry lists every parameter the executor actually reads, the default it falls back to, and what the node does when it goes wrong.

title: What every node on this page has in common
text: A node in this group has three things a Log or a Set Variable node does not: it may need a credential , it may need a capability switched on, and it can fail because of something on the other end of a socket. Understanding those three before reading the individual entries saves repeating them nine times.

title: Credentials are referenced, never stored
text: Any parameter whose type is credentialRef holds the identifier of a stored credential, not the secret itself. The executor resolves it at run time through the secret resolver, so the password, token or connection string never appears in the workflow definition, in an exported bundle, or in a version diff. A blank credentialRef is not an error at compile time — the node simply runs with no secret, which usually surfaces as an authentication failure from the remote server rather than as a Knotarium error.

title: Which nodes are gated, and by what
text: Two different mechanisms gate these nodes, and they live on different settings screens. The coarse on/off switches at Settings › Capabilities cover code execution, database access and the AI agent loop. File access is deliberately not one of those switches — it has its own finer-grained directory policy at Settings › File Access . Everything else on this page runs without a grant. Node Capability tags Gate Needs a credential? HTTP Request network None — descriptive only Only for bearer , basic or apiKey auth Database Query network , database Off by default Privileged — Settings › Capabilities

title: Outbound HTTP goes through the egress policy
text: Every named HTTP client that can reach a user-supplied URL is registered behind the egress guard, and the guard validates twice: once against the literal URI, and once again at the point the socket is opened, pinning the connection to an address it has already vetted. That second check is what stops a redirect hop or a DNS name that resolves to 169.254.169.254 from reaching a private or metadata address after the URL passed inspection. Setting Default Effect on these nodes Security__HttpEgress__DenyPrivateNetworks true Refuses any request that resolves to a private, loopback or link-local addr

title: How the ports behave
text: The ports listed in each entry are the handles you can draw an edge from. Only six node types pick a single branch to follow — Condition, For Loop, Parallel For-Each, AI Router, AI Verify and AI Semantic Diff. Nothing on this page is one of them. When a node here succeeds, the engine schedules every outgoing edge, whichever handle it left. When the node fails, the engine looks for outgoing edges whose handle is named error or failure . If it finds any, it follows those and the run continues; if it finds none, the whole run is marked failed at that node. An error edge also fires on success Beca

title: Automatic retry is narrower than the manifest suggests
text: Several manifests here declare a recovery mode of "retry automatically", but the retry scheduler also requires the node to be marked as an idempotent side effect. A node that changes something on the far end is never retried automatically, no matter what its recovery mode says — re-sending an email or re-running an INSERT because a socket hiccuped is worse than failing. In practice that leaves three nodes on this page with automatic retry. title: HTTP Request
text: The general-purpose way to call something that speaks HTTP. Reach for it when there is no imported OpenAPI specification to generate a typed node from, when you are calling a webhook or a one-off endpoint, or when you need control over the exact headers and body. If you are calling many operations of the same documented API, importing its specification is less work and gives you an operation picker instead of hand-written URLs. Authentication is applied before your custom headers, deliberately: an explicit Authorization header in the headers field overrides whatever the auth block produced, so

title: Imported OpenAPI operations (openapi.<slug>)
text: Importing an OpenAPI specification does not generate one node per endpoint. It generates one node package for the whole specification , whose operationId parameter is a picker over every operation the document declares. Reach for these instead of HTTP Request whenever the API you are calling publishes a specification: you get an operation list, a reusable server configuration holding the base URL and credential, and a version pin. The package id is openapi. followed by the specification's own id lowercased with every character outside a – z , 0 – 9 and - removed; an id that reduces to nothing

title: Database Query
text: Runs one parameterized SQL statement against PostgreSQL or SQLite and hands the rows back as data. Use it for the cases an HTTP API cannot cover: reading a table your organisation already maintains, or writing a row as the last step of a workflow. Anything more elaborate than a single statement belongs in a stored procedure or a view that this node then calls. Values are always bound as database parameters and never concatenated into the statement text, which is what makes the node injection-safe. Write @name in the query and supply name under Parameters ; the key may be written with or withou

title: File Read
text: Reads one local file and emits its contents. Use utf8 when the file is text you want to parse or match on, and base64 when it is binary — an image, a PDF, a zip — that you intend to pass through to an attachment or an upload without interpreting it. Deny by default, and it is not the Capabilities screen A fresh instance grants no directories at all, so every read is denied until an administrator adds one at Settings › File Access . The check happens before any I/O: the requested path is made absolute, every symlink and junction along it is resolved to its real target, and the result must sit i

title: AI nodes
text: Five nodes put a language model inside a workflow: one that runs a single prompt, three that turn a model's judgement into a branch, and one that lets a model call your other workflows as tools. The three branching nodes are the interesting ones — the model does the linguistic work and returns structured data, but the decision about which edge to follow is made by ordinary deterministic code. This page documents every parameter, every port, and where the boundary between the model and the code actually sits.

title: What every AI node needs
text: All five nodes call the instance-wide provider configured at Settings › AI Provider — the vendor, the model and the encrypted API-key credential live there, not on the node. Until that is set up, every AI node fails at run time with the same message: "The AI provider is not configured. Choose a provider, model, and API-key credential in Settings › AI Provider." Nothing fails at design time, so a workflow containing AI nodes saves, publishes and looks healthy on an instance that has never been given a key. Every AI node also declares the network capability, which is descriptive metadata and is

title: AI Prompt
text: One model call over the incoming data. Reach for it when a step needs language understanding rather than logic: summarizing a ticket, extracting fields from free text, drafting a reply, classifying something into a value you will use as data rather than as a branch. If the answer needs to choose an edge , use AI Router instead — it is built for that and does not require you to compare strings downstream. The node runs in one of two modes. Left alone it is a text node: the model's reply is emitted verbatim on result . Fill in jsonSchema and it becomes a structured node: the schema is appended t

title: Branching nodes
text: AI Router, AI Verify and AI Semantic Diff are three of the six node types in Knotarium that select a single outgoing branch rather than following every edge. Each emits an internal selectedPort value, and the engine schedules only the edges whose handle matches it. Draw one edge per branch you care about; branches with no edge simply end that path.

title: AI Router
text: Classifies the incoming text into one of the labels you list, and routes the run down the matching branch. Reach for it when the decision is genuinely linguistic — "is this support email a bug report, a billing question or spam?" — and a Condition or a Switch would need a pile of brittle keyword matching to approximate it. This node's output ports are dynamic The manifest declares no outputs at all . The canvas derives the handles from the node's own categories property: one port per label, in the order you wrote them, followed by a fixed otherwise port. Editing the categories field re-draws t

title: AI Verify
text: An evidence gate. Give it a piece of content and the sources it is supposed to be based on, and it checks the content's factual claims against those sources claim by claim, then routes by the overall verdict. The obvious use is guarding an AI-generated draft before it is sent or published: generate with AI Prompt, verify against the retrieved source documents, and send only down the verified branch. The verdict is code, not a second opinion This is deliberately not "ask another model whether the first one looks right". The model is only asked to do what models are good at — extract each distin

title: AI Semantic Diff
text: Compares two versions of a document by meaning rather than by characters, and routes by whether anything meaningful actually changed. The use it is built for is watching something that gets re-published constantly with cosmetic churn — terms of service, a supplier price list, a policy page — and only waking a human when a deadline, a number or an obligation moves. Identical input never reaches the model Before anything else, the node compares the two inputs after trimming surrounding whitespace. If they are identical it routes straight to none with no model call at all — no tokens, no latency,

title: AI Agent
text: A bounded tool-use loop where the tools are your own workflows . You give the agent a task and an explicit list of workflows it may call; on each turn the model either answers or asks to call one of those workflows with arguments, the workflow runs as a real journaled child run, and its projected outputs are fed back for the next turn. Reach for it when the sequence of steps genuinely cannot be drawn in advance — "find out why this order is late", where the answer might need the order lookup, or the shipment lookup, or both, depending on what the first one returned. When the sequence is known,

title: Defining a tool
text: Each entry in the allowlist binds one of your workflows to a model-facing name. The name must be 1–64 characters of letters, digits and underscores; duplicates and empty target workflows are rejected when the node starts rather than at the first call, so a misconfigured agent fails fast. Field Effect target workflow Which workflow this tool runs. Its published, active version is what executes. name What the model sees and calls. Letters, digits and underscores only. description The only thing telling the model when this tool is the right one. Vague descriptions are the usual cause of an agent

title: What a workflow must look like to be a tool
text: Eligibility is checked at call time, not at design time, so an ineligible workflow shows up as a tool error in the run rather than as a validation message on the canvas. A workflow must: have a published, active version — an unpublished draft is not callable; exist, not be archived, and be enabled; begin with a plain Start node , and contain no Webhook, Polling, Cron Scheduler or Error trigger. A tool has to be a callable function, not an event handler; contain no AI Agent node of its own. The no-nested-agent rule is enforced twice. The tool workflow's nodes are inspected before the child run

title: Why an injected instruction is contained
text: Everything an agent reads is untrusted: the task may contain data from a webhook, and tool results come from workflows that fetched who-knows-what. The default preamble tells the model to treat all of it as data, but a prompt instruction is a mitigation, not a boundary — assume it can be talked around. The actual containment is structural, and it is worth stating precisely because it is what makes the node safe to enable. title: Utility nodes
text: The small nodes that make a workflow legible and debuggable — writing to the run log, setting variables, and dropping to C# when the built-in nodes run out. Plus two nodes that never execute at all, because they exist purely to make the canvas readable, and the External Device block whose ports come from a plugin rather than from a manifest.

title: Everyday utilities
text: Log, Set Variable and Set Variables share a shape: no capabilities, no credentials, a ten-second default timeout, and a recovery mode of "fail immediately" — none of them is ever retried automatically, because none of them can fail for a transient reason. If one of these fails, running it again will fail the same way.

title: Log
text: Writes a message into the application log and the run journal. Reach for it while you are building — dropping a Log between two nodes is the fastest way to see what is actually flowing along an edge, and the message it wrote is preserved in the run history rather than only in the moment. Parameter Type Required {{ }} Default Effect message string no yes log message What to write. An empty or unset message logs the literal text log message rather than an empty line, so an unconfigured Log node is visible in the journal instead of invisible. title: Set Variable
text: Writes one global variable. Use it to carry a value across a branch, to accumulate something in a loop, or to name an expression once instead of repeating it in five nodes. Its real power is that the variable name may be a path , so you can build up a structured object piece by piece rather than assembling JSON in a string. title: Inline Code
text: A short C# script typed straight into the node, filling the gap between an expression — which can only read — and authoring a whole custom node package. Reach for it when a transformation is genuinely awkward to express with the data nodes: parsing an unusual format, a computation with real branching, or reshaping a payload into something a downstream API expects. Anything you reach for repeatedly across workflows deserves to become a node package instead. title: What the script can see
text: The body you type is wrapped in a method, so you write statements rather than a class. Inside it you have Input.Get<T>(name, defaultValue) for the node's inputs (deserialized case-insensitively, falling back to the default rather than throwing on a mismatch), Logger for structured logging, context for workflow state, HTTP and credentials, and cancellationToken . Two helpers end the script: Success(payload) and Fail(message) . A script that never returns is treated as a successful side-effect-only run. Returning an object spreads its properties into top-level outputs and exposes the whole value

title: The timeout is thirty seconds, and how it bites depends on the sandbox
text: Execution is bounded at 30 seconds by default; the manifest's declared timeout is derived from the same shared constant, so the catalog and the executor can never disagree. A node-level timeoutSeconds property overrides the manifest value the engine uses. On expiry the node fails with "Inline Code timed out after 30s". In-process, the timeout is cooperative In the default in-process mode the deadline is a cancellation signal. title: Where the code runs
text: Settings › Sandbox decides whether user-authored C# — this node and compiled custom node packages — runs inside the main process or in pooled worker processes with operating-system limits. The choice is read at every execution , so flipping it takes effect on the next run: no restart, no redeploy. The worker pool is created lazily on the first execution in process mode and kept alive afterwards. title: Annotations that never execute
text: Two node types exist only to make the canvas readable. They have no parameters and no ports , they are never reached by the executor, and they are registered in the node catalog purely so the compiler recognises the type and they round-trip through save, version and restore like any other node. Neither appears in the palette: both are filtered out by id, because they are inserted from the canvas toolbar instead of being dragged.

title: Sticky Note
text: A free-text card you drop on the canvas to explain why something is wired the way it is. Use it for the reasoning that will not survive in your head — why this retry count, which team owns the endpoint, what the ticket number was. The note button on the canvas toolbar inserts a card at the centre of the current viewport, already selected so you can start typing. It defaults to 220 × 150 pixels and is resizable. Five colours are available — amber (the default), green, blue, pink and slate — each rendered as a translucent wash so the canvas grid shows through rather than as a solid block.

title: Group
text: A visual container that wraps a set of nodes into a labelled, collapsible box. Reach for it when a workflow has grown past the point where the shape is obvious — collapsing a finished sub-section removes it from view without removing it from the run. Groups are created from the canvas toolbar's group action over the current selection, and at least two top-level nodes must be selected — the action does nothing with fewer. A group can later be collapsed or ungrouped, which restores its children to the top level. Grouping is purely visual Membership is carried by each child's metadata, not by the

title: External Device and nodes from other packages
External Device
text: A generic, configuration-driven block representing one device or instance managed by an installed provider plugin. It is how a workflow reacts to something happening in the physical or third-party world: you pick a target, tick the signals you care about, and each ticked signal becomes a pin you can wire into ordinary nodes. title: Templates
text: A template is one workflow packaged as a portable file with its credentials removed. Use the built-in gallery to start from a working example, save your own workflows into a library you can reinstall later, and hand a .kgtpl to a colleague knowing it cannot possibly contain one of your passwords. This page covers all four tabs of the Templates screen.

title: The four tabs
text: Templates opens on Browse and offers four tabs, in this order: Tab What it is Browse The read-only gallery of starter templates shipped with the application. Nothing you do here can change it. Library Templates you saved on this instance. Stored in the database, installable and deletable. Import Upload a .kgtpl from somewhere else, inspect it, and create a workflow from it. Export Package one of your workflows as a .kgtpl , or save it straight into the Library. Choosing Export as template from the editor jumps to this screen with the Export tab already selected and the workflow preselected, so

title: What is inside a .kgtpl
text: A template file is a zip with the extension .kgtpl and the media type application/vnd.knotarium.template+zip . For the current format — schema version 1 — the archive contains exactly two entries and nothing else: Entry Contents template.json The manifest: name, author, description, tags, category, template version, creation timestamp, the workflow checksum, the declared credential slots and the declared parameters. workflow.json The exported workflow graph, with every credential reference already replaced by a slot: placeholder. The closed entry set is enforced on read: an archive carrying a

title: Content limits
text: Reading a template bounds the work before anything is deserialized into live types, so a hostile file fails fast instead of exhausting memory: Limit Value Maximum JSON nesting depth 64 Maximum nodes in the workflow 2000 Maximum properties on one node 200 After those checks, the checksum recorded in template.json is recomputed from workflow.json and compared. A mismatch reports that the archive may be corrupt or tampered with, and the import stops. Note what this check does and does not buy you: it detects accidental corruption and casual edits, but since the checksum travels inside the same fi

title: Browse — installing from the gallery
text: The gallery is built from reviewable, unzipped sources shipped next to the application rather than from committed binaries, and each entry is packed into a consistent archive on demand. Every built-in template in the current build carries the category starter , the author Knotarium , and version 1.0.0 : Template What it demonstrates Hello World A manual trigger that logs a greeting and ends — the smallest thing worth running. Log Run Markers A start marker and a finish marker around an empty middle step, as a scaffold for your own logic. Set and Use a Variable Storing a value and reading it ba

title: The install form
text: Each card shows the name, the author, the template version, the description, its tags, and a count of how many credential slots it declares. The first click on Use template does not install anything — it expands the card into the install form. The button then reads Create workflow , and that second click is the one that creates something. The form has up to three parts, and only the first is always present: Workflow name — prefilled with the template's name and editable. Parameters — one input per declared parameter, shown only when the template declares any. Credential slots — one binding row

title: Parameters
text: A parameter is a non-secret value the template's author left blank for you to supply: a channel name, a base URL, a polling interval. The workflow references it with a {{param:<key>}} token, and the token is replaced with your value as the workflow is created. Four types exist, and each renders a different input: Type Input Accepted string Text box Anything. number Number box Parsed with invariant culture, so the decimal separator is a full stop regardless of your locale. boolean Dropdown true or false . enum Dropdown One of the options the author declared. Required parameters are marked with

title: Credential slot binding
text: This is the mechanism that makes sharing a workflow safe. When a workflow is exported, every node property whose value is one of your credential ids is replaced with a symbolic token slot:<key> , and the manifest declares one slot per distinct credential. The slot carries a display name and, optionally, a description and a required credential type. It never carries the credential itself, the credential's id, or anything derived from its secret value. Export lifts credential ids into slots; install binds those slots to credentials that exist on your own instance. Slot keys are derived from the

title: Previewing before you install
text: The expanded card carries a Preview button that renders the template's graph as a read-only mini-canvas: one card per node showing its label and its node type, laid out left-to-right, with the edges drawn between them. It is deliberately inert — no dragging, panning, zooming or selecting. The preview is generated from the template with your current parameter values already substituted, so it shows what you are about to create rather than the raw template. It does not create a workflow, and it is fetched fresh each time you open it. Pressing the button again hides it.

title: Import — installing someone else's template
text: The Import tab takes a .kgtpl by clicking the drop zone or dragging a file onto it. The file is inspected immediately, before anything is created: the manifest is parsed, the checksum verified, the graph compiled to assess compatibility, and the node types scanned for privileged capabilities. Nothing is written to the database during inspection. The inspection panel then shows: The template's name, author and version. A compatibility badge, either Runs here or Check compatibility . The number of credential slots, and that it installs as a draft. The privileged-node acknowledgement, when applic

title: The privileged-node acknowledgement
text: Inspection resolves every distinct node type in the template against its package manifest and collects the ones declaring a privileged capability — filesystem access, code execution, or database access. If any are found, an amber panel appears listing each privileged node by its display name together with the capabilities it carries, followed by a checkbox reading I understand and want to install this template. Until that box is ticked, Create workflow stays disabled and a line beside it reads that you must acknowledge the warning. The prompt appears on the Import tab only, because that is the

title: Export — packaging a workflow
text: Export packages a workflow's currently published state . This matters: unsaved canvas edits and unpublished drafts are not what gets exported, and a workflow that has never been published has nothing to export — the attempt reports that no version is available. The form collects the metadata that will be shown to whoever installs the result: Field Default when left blank Workflow Required; there is no default. Template name The workflow's own name. Also determines the file name. Author Empty. Description Empty. Tags Empty. Entered as a comma-separated list. Category uncategorized . Version 1.0

title: Library — your own saved templates
text: The Library tab lists templates saved on this instance, most recently saved first. Templates arrive there in two ways: Save to library on the Export tab, which packs one of your workflows, and Save to library on the Import tab, which stores an archive someone sent you. In both cases the archive is verified before it is stored, so a corrupt file is refused rather than persisted. Each library card installs exactly like a gallery card: Use template expands the install form, Create workflow creates the draft, and Preview renders the graph. Each card also carries a Delete button, which removes the

title: What installing never does
text: Two properties are worth stating explicitly, because they bound the risk of accepting a template from someone else: An install always creates a new workflow under a new id. It never modifies, overwrites or deletes a workflow you already have, even when the names collide. The imported workflow is created inactive . Nothing about installing a template causes anything to run: you still have to publish it, enable it, and have the runtime armed. Bundles Multi-package integration bundles, and the signing that lets you verify who published one. Configuration reference Where exported files are written

title: Bundles
text: A bundle is an integration shipped as one file: several workflows, the custom node packages they depend on, a lock recording exactly which package bytes were meant, and a declaration of the credentials the recipient must supply. Where a template is a convenience, a bundle is a supply chain — which is why installing one runs a verification gate that can refuse the whole thing. Bundles has two tabs, Install and Export.

title: Bundle or template?
text: Both formats carry workflows and both use the same slot: credential placeholders, so the choice comes down to what else needs to travel: Template ( .kgtpl ) Bundle ( .kgbundle ) Workflows Exactly one Any number Node packages None Every non-built-in package the workflows use Dependency lock None bundle.lock , with a hash per package Signatures None Per package, verified on install Credential handling Credentials are stripped into slots automatically on export Slots are declared by hand; export does not rewrite credential ids Install parameters Typed {{param:…}} values None Failure mode Imports

title: What is inside a .kgbundle
text: A .kgbundle is a zip written deterministically — entries in a stable order with a fixed timestamp — so identical contents always produce identical bytes and therefore an identical hash. Its layout is: Entry Contents bundle.json The manifest: authoring intent. Bundle id, version, name, publisher, tags, category, schema version, minimum engine version, the package references, the declared credential slots, the workflow references, and the claimed provenance. Deliberately carries no hashes. bundle.lock The resolved record: for every package, its resolved version, its SHA-256, the source it resolv

title: Export — assembling a bundle
text: The Export tab builds the manifest from four sections, then asks the server to resolve and pack it.

title: Metadata

It also becomes the file name stem. Version Defaults to 1.0.0 ; an empty value is packed as 0.0.0 . Name Falls back to the bundle id when left blank. Publisher Free text. Recorded in the manifest and in the claimed provenance. Category Free text. Tags Comma-separated. title: Workflows
text: A checklist of every workflow on the instance, with Select all and Clear all . At least one must be selected or the export is refused. Each selected workflow becomes a manifest entry with the role primary , and its exported document is written into the archive under its own id.

title: Packages — derived, not chosen

Every node's type is a package id, so the bundle's package set is computed from the node types used by the workflows you selected, and the panel updates as you tick workflows on and off. Two filters apply: Built-in node types drop out. They ship with the engine, carry no installable registry version, and cannot be bundled — if your workflows use only built-in nodes, the panel says so and the bundle contains no packages at all. Each remaining package is pinned to an installed version whose source is not a built-in one — the panel describes this as its latest installe

text: Add credential slot appends a row with two fields: the slot key — the slot:<name> placeholder the bundled workflows are expected to use — and a human-readable label shown to whoever installs the bundle. A row with an empty key is dropped when the manifest is built, and the label defaults to the key when left blank. Bundle export does not remove your credentials This is the single most important difference from a template. Template export walks every node property and rewrites credential references into slots automatically. Bundle export does not. Workflows are packed exactly as they are, so a

title: Signing
text: Bundle trust rests entirely on the signatures carried by the individual node packages inside it. Two configuration settings govern the two directions. Setting Direction Effect Security__PackageSigning__HostPrivateKeyBase64 Outbound The Ed25519 private key this host signs node packages with. It must be valid base64 decoding to exactly 32 bytes; a key that is missing, not base64, or the wrong length makes publishing fail with a server error naming which of the three it was. Security__PackageSigning__TrustedPublicKeys Inbound The list of public keys whose signatures this host accepts. Empty by de

title: Install — the verification gate
text: The Install tab takes a .kgbundle by click or drag-and-drop, offers an Allow provisional installs toggle, and installs on the button. What happens next is a sequence of gates, each of which must pass before the next runs, with every database write held until the end: Every gate runs before any write. A rejected install leaves the registry exactly as it was.

title: What verification actually re-derives
text: The installer does not take the lock's word for anything. For each package listed in the lock it finds the matching file under packages/ , recomputes the hash from the carried payload, compares it against the lock, re-checks the signature against your trusted keys — which may differ entirely from the exporter's — and re-derives the trust level from that result. The lock is a claim to be checked, not a verdict to be accepted. Trust is derived from two inputs, the signature verdict and the package's resolved source: Trust level How a package earns it Installable? Verified Its signature verified

title: The verification report
text: Whatever the outcome, a table appears listing every locked package with six columns — Package, Trust, Signature, Hash, Status and Installable — and the rows that blocked the install are highlighted. Signature and Status are kept as separate axes on purpose, because they answer different questions: Signature column Meaning No signature The package file carries no signature at all. Untrusted signature A signature is present but did not verify against any of your trusted keys. As noted above, this covers both an invalid signature and a valid one from an untrusted signer.
