The install is rejected with 422 and nothing is written until you tick Allow provisional installs and install again. This is the normal path for a package a colleague built in their own node editor. Unsigned but claiming a non-local source. Trust is Untrusted, and the provisional toggle does not help — there is no configuration that makes it installable. To install it you must obtain a properly signed build, or add the publisher's public key to TrustedPublicKeys and

title: The privileged-node acknowledgement
text: Once verification passes, every node across every bundled workflow is resolved against its package manifest and any privileged capability — filesystem, code execution, database — is collected. If anything is found and you have not acknowledged it, the install stops there and writes nothing. Because the scan happens server-side, the warning appears after your first install attempt rather than on upload: an amber panel lists each privileged node with its capabilities and offers I understand and want to install this bundle , and the primary button changes to Re-install . Tick the box and press it

title: Version conflicts
text: The last check before any write compares each locked package against what is already in the registry. If a package at that exact version is installed but its bytes hash differently from the lock, the whole install is rejected with a conflict banner naming the packages, and nothing is written. This refusal is the point. Skipping such a package as "already installed" would quietly bind the bundle's workflows to a different build of the same version number, which is the sort of failure that surfaces weeks later as behaviour nobody can reproduce. The result carries the slots the manifest declares, and a Credential slots card appears with one dropdown per slot, defaulting to leave unbound . Choose credentials and install again. Leaving a slot unbound is allowed. The imported workflows keep the literal slot:<name> placeholder, the success banner lists the unbound slots in amber, and you can either re-install with bindings or set the credentials on the workflows directly. title: Importing OpenAPI
text: Point Knotarium at an API's own description and it generates a node for that API — one node per specification, with every operation available as a dropdown value. This is the fastest route from "we have an internal REST service" to "a workflow calls it", and it replaces hand-assembling URLs, headers and authentication in an HTTP Request node. The screen is API Importer .

title: How the screen is laid out
text: API Importer is split into a narrow left panel and a main area, with two modes selected by the panel's own tabs: APIs — the list of imported specifications, with an Import Spec button above it. Selecting one fills the main area with its operation browser. Server Configs — the manager for the base URLs and authentication settings the generated nodes call through. The two halves are separate on purpose. A specification says what an API can do; a server configuration says which instance of it you are talking to and with what credential. One imported specification can be pointed at staging and at

title: Importing a specification
text: Import Spec opens a dialog offering three routes, all of which end in the same parse. OpenAPI 3.0, OpenAPI 3.1 and Swagger 2.0 are accepted, in either JSON or YAML. Tab Use it when Paste Content You have the document in your clipboard. This is the default tab. Upload File You have a file. Click the drop zone or drag a file onto it; the picker filters to .json , .yaml and .yml . From URL The API publishes its own specification. Enter an absolute http or https URL.

title: Fetching by URL
text: The fetch happens on the server rather than in your browser, which is what makes cross-origin specification URLs work at all — most API hosts do not send the CORS headers a browser would demand. A URL that is not absolute, or that uses a scheme other than http or https , is rejected before any request is made, and a non-success response or an empty body is reported as an import failure rather than being stored. Because the request goes out from the server, it goes through exactly the same egress policy as an HTTP Request node. With the default Security__HttpEgress__DenyPrivateNetworks setting

title: The spec ID field
text: Every import accepts an optional Spec ID . Left blank, the identity is derived from the specification's title: lower-cased, with every run of characters outside a–z and 0–9 collapsed to a hyphen and leading and trailing hyphens trimmed. An explicit value is slugified by the same rule. Two APIs with the same title merge into one version history The identity is the title slug, so importing two genuinely different APIs that both call themselves "API" makes the second one look like a new version of the first. Nothing warns you; the earlier specification simply becomes an old version of a spec now

title: Browsing what was imported
text: Selecting a specification in the left panel shows its title, its declared API version, and the current internal version number, above a browser with two tabs. Each tab carries a count badge.

title: Operations
text: Operations are grouped by their OpenAPI tag, with one collapsible section per tag showing how many operations it holds. Every group starts expanded. Each row shows the HTTP method as a colour-coded badge — green for GET, blue for POST, amber for PUT, red for DELETE, violet for PATCH, grey for HEAD and for anything unrecognised — followed by the path template and, where the specification supplies one, the operation's summary. Operation rows are draggable . Dragging one onto the canvas creates a node of the generated package with that operation already selected and an empty argument object, whic

title: Schemas
text: The Schemas tab lists the named schemas the specification defines, one card each, showing the schema name and its description. View JSON expands the card to show the schema pretty-printed; if the stored text is not valid JSON it is shown verbatim rather than failing. The tab is read-only — it exists so you can check the shape of a request body or response while authoring, without leaving the application.

title: What an import generates
text: Importing does two things: it stores the parsed specification as a new version, and it generates a node package so the API shows up in the palette. The package is generated deterministically from the specification — the same document always produces the same package. One import, two artefacts: a versioned specification record and a regenerated node package.

title: The generated package
text: The package id is openapi. followed by the specification's slug with every character outside a–z , 0–9 and - stripped out. A specification whose slug reduces to nothing becomes openapi.spec . text: The delete button on a specification row asks for confirmation and warns that it removes the specification and all its imported versions permanently. Workflows that reference the generated package are not consulted.

Set its Source Kind to openapi and the form swaps its HTTP fields for three OpenAPI ones: Server Config — required; the same list the generated nodes use, each entry showing its name and base URL. Only the server configuration and the operation are saved on the node. The specification

title: Importing configurations
text: The Import screen reads a configuration file exported from another vendor's system and translates it into Knotarium workflows. It is a migration tool: you hand it someone else's automation, it tells you honestly how much of that automation it could express, and it lands the result as inactive drafts you review before anything is allowed to run. Nothing about this screen is reversible-by-accident — there is a dry run, and there is an undo.

title: What this screen needs before it works
text: The importer is a generic shell around a plugin. Knotarium itself understands no vendor format whatsoever; a host plugin supplies a source-format provider that knows how to parse one. With no plugin installed, the screen shows a single message — that no import providers are registered and that you need to install a connection-manager plugin that ships one — and nothing else on this page applies. Plugins are loaded at startup from the folder named by NodeRuntime__PluginsPath , which defaults to a plugins folder beside the application. Each plugin lives in its own subfolder. Adding one means res

title: The three steps
text: A stepper across the top tracks where you are: Upload file , Configure , then Review coverage . Uploading a file advances to Configure; previewing or importing advances to Review coverage. Removing the file returns you to the start and clears every choice you made. Preview and import share the same configuration; only import writes anything.

title: Step 1 — choosing a source format and a file
text: When more than one provider is installed, a Source format dropdown appears above the drop zone listing each provider by its display name. With exactly one provider the dropdown is hidden and that provider is selected automatically. Changing the source format resets the whole form, because a file parsed by one provider means nothing to another. The drop zone accepts a click or a drag-and-drop. The file picker is filtered to the extensions the selected provider declares, and those extensions are also printed on the chip below the drop zone next to the provider's name — so the screen tells you wh

Option What you get One combined workflow Every flow in the file lands in a single workflow as independent chains, side by side on one canvas. Separate workflows One workflow per flow. Each is published, armed and managed on its own. The provider chooses which one is preselected, and the preselection is re-applied whenever you change provider. Vendor configuration files typically default to the combined option, for a prac

title: Device connections
text: Vendor configurations usually address physical devices or servers. When the provider declares that it references external systems and the parse discovered at least one, a Device connections section appears, headed with the count and listing the discovered aliases. Three strategies are offered: Strategy What it does Create automatically Makes a connection target for each referenced server, reusing any existing target with the same name instead of duplicating it. This is the default. Map to existing Binds each referenced server to a connection target you already have. One dropdown per alias, eac

Each entry is an alias, an action, and where applicable the target it resolves to: Action Meaning Create A new connection target will be created for this alias. Reuse An existing target with a matching name will be used as-is. Bind The alias will be bound to the target you selected. Skip Nothing will be provisioned for this alias. title: The dry run
text: Preview re-parses the file with your current options and switches to the coverage view without writing anything. The banner reads Preview , states how many workflows would be produced and whether they would be combined or separate, and says explicitly that this is a dry run and nothing has been imported. The dry run is genuinely side-effect free — provisioning is switched off for it at the contract level, so even the Create actions in the plan are hypothetical. From the preview you can go Back to change your options, or Import to commit without re-reading the report.

title: The coverage report
text: The report is the reason this screen exists. Every construct the provider encountered gets one row, including the ones it could not translate — the contract states that a construct with no analogue is surfaced here and never silently dropped. Four columns: Column Contents Scope Where in the source file the construct came from, in monospace — the provider's own coordinate for it. Construct What it was. Bare numbers in this text — device and sequence identifiers — are highlighted, and a plain -> is rendered as an arrow, so relationships are readable at a glance. Outcome A colour-coded pill: Mapp

title: Importing
text: Import runs the same translation with provisioning switched on, creates the connection targets the plan described, and installs each generated workflow as an inactive Imported version. The success banner reports how many workflows were imported and whether they were combined or separate, repeats that they are inactive drafts that will not run until you publish and arm them, and lists any connection targets that were created along with the reminder to set their passwords. The coverage report stays on screen after the import, now reflecting the committed run, with three actions in its footer: Un

title: Collision handling
text: Providers assign their own workflow ids, and those ids are not necessarily unique across imports — a provider that produces one workflow per file may well use the same fixed id every time. Left alone, importing a second configuration would file it as a hidden new version of the first rather than as its own workflow. The importer prevents that. Before installing, it reads the ids and names already in the database and, for each workflow whose id collides, mints a fresh id and appends a numeric suffix to the name until it is free — so a second import of a configuration named Building A installs a

title: Undoing an import
text: Undo import is offered in the report footer immediately after a successful import, labelled with the number of workflows it will remove. It archives every workflow the import created, in one call, and the banner then reads that the import was undone and how many workflows were removed. The button disappears once used. "Archives" is the precise word. A workflow that has versions is marked archived and its draft removed, rather than being erased — archived workflows are hidden from the dashboard list but can be restored, which un-archives the header and rebuilds its draft from the latest version

title: After the import
text: Everything the importer creates is inert. In order for an imported workflow to do anything, three separate things have to happen, and the importer does none of them: Any connection target the import created needs its password set under Settings › External Systems . The workflow needs to be published — an imported version is created but not made active. The runtime needs to be armed, and the workflow enabled, before a trigger will fire. That ordering is worth respecting. Publishing before the targets are online produces a workflow that publishes cleanly and fails on its first run, which is a mo

title: Settings overview
text: Everything an administrator changes at runtime lives on one screen, split into eight sections. This page is the map: what each section is responsible for, how quickly a change takes hold, and the one rule that catches people out — several of these screens write their values into the database, where they permanently outrank the same settings in appsettings.json .

title: File Access
text: Deny-by-default directory grants for the two file nodes, a free-space reserve that blocks writes which would fill the drive, and an escape hatch that grants unrestricted access. On a fresh instance nothing is granted, so every file operation fails until you allow a path. See File access .

title: Capabilities
text: Master switches for the privileged capabilities that have no finer-grained policy of their own. Turning one on is an instance-wide grant: every workflow can use it, including workflows that arrived by import or were generated by a language model. See Capabilities .

title: Sandbox
text: Complements Capabilities. Where that screen decides whether user-authored C# may run, this one decides how safely : in the backend process, or in pooled worker processes with operating-system limits on memory, CPU, run time and privileges. See Sandbox .

title: Retention
text: Two cards on one page. Data retention prunes old finished runs and their journals, and optionally caps version histories and the audit log. Disk-space guard is the backstop underneath it: when free space on the data volume drops below a floor, the runtime is disarmed so no new runs start. See Retention and disk space .

title: External Systems

For each target you configure a name, host, port and optional user with a stored password, and the manager adds three operations: Test checks connectivity before you save, Sync refreshes the live catalog of channels, events and actions that the canvas editor offers, and delete removes the target after a confirmation. text: Not a settings screen at all, but instance-level data management: it downloads a complete encrypted snapshot of the instance including its secrets, and performs the destructive restore. It is deliberately kept on its own page rather than sharing a screen with a webhook test button. See Backup and restore .

title: Security model
text: Knotarium exists to run code and touch systems on your behalf. That makes a running instance a privileged thing, and the question that matters is not which nodes exist but who can author, import or trigger a workflow. This page sets out that trust boundary, walks through each layer of defence that backs it up, and is deliberately honest about what the product does not yet protect against.

title: The trust boundary
text: Everything else on this page follows from one sentence: anyone who can author, import or trigger a workflow can potentially run code on the host. The engine compiles real C# at runtime, opens database connections, reads and writes local files, makes outbound HTTP calls and sends mail. Those are the product's features, not accidents, and no in-application control makes an untrusted author safe. The layered defences below are therefore about two things: making the dangerous capabilities off until deliberately enabled , and limiting the blast radius when something does go wrong. They are not a su

title: The layers
text: A request arriving at the instance passes through the network and session controls; a workflow reaching outward or downward passes through the capability, filesystem, sandbox and egress controls. The diagram below reads top to bottom in the order the checks actually happen. Each layer fails closed. None of them makes an untrusted workflow author safe.

title: Authentication
text: Cookie sign-in is on by default. On a fresh instance with no accounts the browser is shown a first-run screen that creates the initial administrator, so an unconfigured instance is reachable but immediately secured. Authorization is deny-by-default: a fallback policy requires an authenticated user on every endpoint, and only a short list opts out — the sign-in bootstrap routes, the machine-facing webhook trigger and resume, and the single-page application shell itself so the login screen can render before a session exists. text: Authentication can be turned off with Auth__Enabled=false . In that mode there is no authentication middleware at all and every endpoint is anonymous — including the capability toggle and the Inline Code test endpoint. That combination is only defensible when the server can be reached from the local machine alone. So the composition root checks it. At startup, with authentication disabled, the configured binding addresses are inspected and any non-loopback address is collected. title: Rate limiting
text: Two surfaces are abuse-prone and both are throttled with a per-client fixed window, where the client is identified by its remote IP address. Rejections are answered with 429 Too Many Requests , and nothing is queued — a request over the limit is refused outright rather than delayed. A request with no Origin header at all passes, which is why this is defence in depth layered on top of the SameSite=Lax session cookie rather than a complete cross-site request forgery defence on its own. The policy lives in the database, an unset or unparseable value means everything is off, and the fallback implementation wired into a host that never registers the real store reports every capability as disabled. Every path fails closed. Filesystem access is deliberately excluded from that coarse switch because it has its own finer-grained policy. A fresh instance grants nothing, so every file operation is denied until an administrator allows a directory. Within an enforced policy the guard is strict: a relative path is refused outright rather than resolved against an unpredictable working directory, textual .. is collapsed, and every symlink and junction along the path's existing prefix is resolved to its real target before the result is boundary-checked against the granted roots. title: The HTTP egress policy
text: Every outbound request the engine makes — the HTTP Request node, AI provider calls, anything a sandboxed script proxies through the host — is checked against an egress policy. The default posture blocks server-side request forgery against your own internal network. With Security__HttpEgress__DenyPrivateNetworks left at its default of true, a destination is refused when it is private, loopback, link-local or otherwise not publicly routable. text: Checking the literal hostname is not enough, because a hostname that looks public can resolve to an internal address. So the policy resolves the host itself and validates every candidate address before connecting, then pins the connection to an address it approved . Because this runs in the connection callback, it happens for the initial request and again for every redirect hop, and there is no window between checking and connecting in which a rebound record could take effect. text: Two optional domain lists narrow things further. The block-list is checked first and always refuses. The allow-list, when non-empty, restricts outbound traffic to those domains only; left empty, no allow-list is applied. Both match a host exactly or as a subdomain, and a leading *. in a pattern is stripped, so *.example.com and example.com behave identically — both match the domain itself and everything beneath it. On install the signature is verified against Security__PackageSigning__TrustedPublicKeys , and a package that fails verification is rejected outright. A resolved package lands in one of three trust levels. Verified means its signature checked out against a trusted key, which is sufficient regardless of where it came from. If any are found, the install is blocked and returns the list of offending nodes with the capabilities each one carries. Left unconfigured, one is generated into .credential-key in the data directory on first use and reused forever after; you can supply your own with Security__Credentials__EncryptionKeyBase64 , but changing it afterwards makes every saved secret unreadable. title: Exposing an instance to a network
text: The honest guidance is short. Do not put an instance directly on the public internet. Cookie authentication being on by default is not a substitute for network-level controls, and the product does not yet have the role model that would make a shared, semi-trusted deployment safe. If you must make an instance reachable beyond the machine it runs on: Put it behind a reverse proxy that terminates TLS. Inline code and SQL are not sandboxed by design. They need the runtime compiler and a live connection. title: Capabilities
text: Settings › Capabilities holds the master switches for the privileged things a node can do. They are off on a fresh instance, and a node that needs one fails with a clear message until an administrator turns it on. Each switch is instance-wide: enabling it grants the capability to every workflow on the instance, not to the one you were looking at.

That includes: Workflows other account holders create, since there is no role model that would stop them. Workflows imported from a template or bundle, including ones imported after you flipped the switch. Workflows generated from a natural-language description by a language model. title: File access
text: Settings › File Access decides which directories the File Read and File Write nodes may touch. On a fresh instance the answer is none — every file operation is denied until an administrator grants a path. This page covers granting subtrees, the free-space reserve that stops a workflow filling a drive, the escape hatch you should think twice about, and the one-click remediation offered when a run fails on a denial.

title: Deny by default

With no grants and total access off, the card shows a grey advisory reading No paths granted and total access off — every File Read / File Write will fail until you allow a path , and that is exactly what happens. A run reaching a file node gets a denial naming the path it attempted. This is not the same kind of control as the switches on Capabilities . A grant covers the directory and everything beneath it, recursively — you do not enumerate subfolders. A trash-can button on the right removes a row. Rows are edited freely and nothing is enforced until you press Save policy . The button stays disabled while the form matches what is stored, and the card says No changes beside it; after a successful save it says Saved . title: Sandbox
text: Settings › Sandbox decides where user-authored C# — the Inline Code node and compiled custom node packages — actually executes, and how hard the operating system confines it while it does. It is the companion to Capabilities : that screen decides whether code may run, this one decides how safely .

title: The two modes
text: The card offers a choice of two, presented as radio buttons.

title: In-process (compatible)
text: The default. Scripts run inside the backend process with full access, which is fast — there is no process to start, no data to marshal across a boundary — but means a runaway script can stall or crash the whole instance. An endless loop occupies a thread the engine needed; a memory bomb takes the engine's memory with it; an unhandled fault can take the process down. The timeout is still enforced in this mode, but it is cooperative : a script has to observe the cancellation token it is given for a long operation to be interruptible. A tight loop that never checks will not stop when the timeout

title: Isolated process (recommended)
text: Scripts run in pooled worker processes with operating-system-enforced memory and CPU limits. Endless loops and memory bombs are killed hard and the backend stays up. This is the mode that makes the numeric limits below mean anything, and the only mode in which restricted tokens and credential proxying are available. The trade-off is the one you would expect: a process boundary costs start-up time on a cold worker and marshalling on every call, and a script that relied on touching the host directly may stop working under a restricted token. That second point is the usual reason people leave in-

title: The toggles
text: Three checkboxes sit under the mode selector. Two of them are dimmed and disabled outside process mode, labelled isolated mode only .

title: Screen code before running
text: Rejects scripts that use banned APIs — filesystem, process control and similar — at run time, applying the same check the node editor applies while you are writing. It works in both modes, because it happens before compilation rather than during execution. On by default This is a screening pass, not a sandbox. It stops the obvious calls; it is not a proof that a script cannot reach the host, and it should not be the only thing standing between an untrusted script and your machine.

title: Restricted worker privileges (Windows)
text: Runs workers with stripped privileges and low integrity: no access to user profiles, service data or most of the file system. Under the hood this launches the worker with a restricted token, restricting security identifiers, and a Low integrity level, which denies access to user- and admin-scoped filesystem and registry objects. On by default It is best-effort: if the restricted launch fails, the worker starts normally and a warning is logged rather than the execution being refused. Node code can use a credential but never read one. On by default The interface's advice on turning it off is exact: disable it only for scripts that need the raw value for something other than an HTTP call, such as computing an HMAC signature. title: Retention and disk space
text: Settings › Retention holds two cards that solve the same problem from opposite ends. Data retention bounds how large the database can grow by pruning on a schedule. Disk-space guard is the backstop underneath it: when free space runs out anyway, it disarms the runtime so nothing new starts writing. Neither needs a restart, and neither takes effect instantly.

title: Why this screen exists
text: Every run writes a journal — one entry per step — and that is what makes the run inspector able to replay a run that finished days ago. It is also the fastest-growing table in the product. A once-a-minute schedule adds roughly half a million schedule-fire rows a year on its own, before any journal entries. On a long-lived instance with no retention configured, the SQLite file grows without bound until the disk is full. A full disk does not crash the engine — SQLite starts failing writes and the product degrades rather than falls over — but that is a bad place to arrive at. These two cards are

title: Data retention
text: The card's description is accurate about the essential guarantee: old finished runs are deleted along with their logs, and in-flight runs are never touched . Concretely, only runs in a terminal state are eligible — completed, failed, cancelled or discarded. A run that is pending, running, suspended or waiting to retry is excluded no matter how old it is, so a long-suspended run is never deleted out from under the executor.

title: How a sweep runs

Two consequences follow from that shape: The first sweep is one interval after startup. A process that starts and stops quickly never prunes anything, which is deliberate — an upgrade or a short-lived test run should not silently delete history. The loop never exits when retention is disabled. With everything at zero the sweep returns immediately, but the worker keeps cycling so that turning retention on later is picked up without a restart. Retention only prunes on a schedule and is time-based, so nothing else in the product reacts to a disk approaching full. text: It is easy to confuse this floor with the reserve on File access , and they do different jobs: Disk-space guard File-access reserve Watches The volume holding the data directory The drive each write targets Triggered by A periodic check An individual write, before it happens Effect Disarms the whole runtime Denies that one write Recovery Manual re-arm Automatic once space exists On an instance whose workflows write large files to the same volume as the database, configure both. The reserve stops a single workflow eating the headroom; the guard stops the accumulated journal doing it slowly.

title: Backup and restore
text: Settings › Backup & Restore produces a single encrypted file containing everything this instance manages — including its secrets — and can replace the instance's entire state from one. Because a backup carries decrypted credentials inside its envelope, it is not a shareable artefact and it lives here under instance settings rather than alongside templates and bundles.

title: The file
text: A backup is a single file with the extension .kgbak , named knotarium-backup- followed by the creation timestamp in UTC — for example knotarium-backup-20260725-141203.kgbak . The browser downloads it directly; nothing is written on the server. Inside the envelope is an ordinary zip with a stable layout: a manifest at backup.json , the workflow-group file, one JSON document per database aggregate under data/ , and one file per workflow draft under workflows/ . The zip is written in a canonical order with a pinned timestamp so the same content always produces the same bytes. You never see any of

title: The encryption
text: The envelope is AES-256-GCM. Its header is cleartext — a magic marker, the envelope version, a byte recording how the key was derived, the iteration count and a random salt — and that header is fed to the cipher as associated data, so tampering with the key-derivation parameters makes authentication fail rather than silently changing how the file is read. A wrong passphrase and a corrupted archive are indistinguishable by design: both fail the authentication tag and both produce the message Incorrect passphrase, or the backup archive is corrupt .

title: Creating a backup
text: The left card is headed Create a backup and tagged Safe . It offers two protection modes as a pair of buttons.

title: Passphrase
text: The default and the portable option. The key is derived from your passphrase with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 600,000 iterations — the OWASP-recommended floor, chosen so guessing against a stolen archive is expensive. The iteration count travels in the header so it can be raised in future without breaking older files. You type the passphrase twice. The card requires at least eight characters and a match before the download button enables, and shows a four-segment strength meter labelled Weak, Fair, Good or Strong based on length, mixed case with digits, and the presence of a symbol. A passphrase und

title: This server's key
text: The key is derived with HKDF-SHA256 from this host's credential encryption key, domain-separated so it is not the same key used for anything else. There is no passphrase to remember and nothing to lose — but the archive only decrypts on a host whose credential key is unchanged. That makes it right for automatic local snapshots and useless for migration, by design. If you restore it elsewhere the failure is explicit rather than confusing: a server-key backup only restores on the host that created it . It also means that replacing or losing the credential key makes every server-key backup you ho

title: What is in a backup — and what is not
text: The snapshot covers everything the instance manages as configuration and content: Workflow definitions, their published versions, the active-version pointers and the activation log. Workflow drafts from the file store, and the dashboard's workflow grouping. Schedules and polling triggers. Installed node packages with their versions. Credentials and notification channels. Application settings — which includes the capability policy, the file-access policy, the sandbox and retention settings, and the AI provider configuration. Server configurations and imported OpenAPI specifications with their v

title: How secrets travel
text: This is the part that dictates everything else about the format. Credential values and notification-channel configurations are stored in the database encrypted under this host's at-rest key, which is not in the database. A raw copy of those ciphertexts is undecryptable on a host with a different key — so a backup carries them decrypted inside the encrypted envelope, and the restore re-encrypts them under the target host's key. That is what makes migration between hosts possible at all. It is also exactly why the archive itself must be encrypted and why a backup is not something to leave in a s

title: Restoring
text: The right card is headed Restore from a backup and tagged Destructive , because it is: restoring replaces all current state with the backup's contents. The flow is deliberately stepped so there is no single click that does it.

title: Step one — choose the file
text: Drop a .kgbak on the drop zone or browse for one. As soon as a file is selected the first six bytes are read in the browser to check the magic marker and read the key-source byte, so the card can tell you whether it is passphrase-protected or server-key encrypted without a round-trip and without decrypting anything. The file chip shows the size in megabytes alongside that verdict.

title: Step two — inspect
text: For a passphrase backup you enter the passphrase used when it was created. For a detected server-key backup the field is replaced by a note saying no passphrase is needed and the file opens only on this host. Inspect backup decrypts the archive and parses the manifest only — nothing is written. The preview shows when the backup was created, the engine version with the format version and database provider, and per-aggregate counts: workflows and versions, schedules and polling triggers, credentials and channels, whether run history is included and the file size, and how the archive was encrypte

title: Step three — the two checks
text: A guard block headed Before restoring — 2 checks appears with the preview. Disarm the runtime. Until it is disarmed the step is open and offers a Disarm now button that flips the same shared state the header pill shows. Once disarmed it reads Runtime disarmed — no live triggers will fire during the restore . The safety backup is automatic. This step is always shown as already done, because the current state is snapshotted before any change is made. The disarm requirement is enforced on the server, not just in the interface. A restore attempted while the runtime is armed is refused before any d

title: Step four — type to confirm
text: A field asks you to type RESTORE to confirm the irreversible replace. The field is disabled until the runtime is disarmed, and the Restore this instance button only enables when the preview is present, the runtime is disarmed and the confirmation matches. The server independently requires an explicit confirmation flag and refuses without it, so the typed word is not merely a client-side speed bump.

title: What the restore actually does
text: In order: it resolves the key, decrypts and reads the archive, and checks format compatibility. Then it writes a pre-restore safety backup of the current state, encrypted in the same mode as the incoming archive so it can be opened the same way. Then it decodes every aggregate from the archive up front, so a malformed document fails before anything is deleted. Only then does it open a transaction, clear the managed tables in child-to-parent order, and re-insert everything in parent-to-child order — re-encrypting credentials and channel configurations under the current host's key as it goes. Ru

title: Who may do this
text: All three operations — create, inspect and restore — require the admin role, because a full-instance backup contains every secret in re-encryptable form. This is one of the few places the role check is actually enforced; see Security model for why you should not read more into that than it deserves. On an instance running with authentication disabled the check is a no-op, consistent with every other endpoint being anonymous in that mode.

title: How this relates to a file-level backup
text: Copying files off the disk is a perfectly reasonable backup strategy, and for a stopped instance it captures more than a .kgbak does — run history and user accounts included. But it has one failure mode that loses data permanently, and it is the single most important thing on this page. The database and the credential key must be backed up together Knotarium.db holds every credential as ciphertext. .credential-key — sitting beside it in the data directory — is what decrypts them. A copy of the database without that key leaves you with credentials that can never be read again: not by you, not b

title: Users and sign-in
text: Cookie sign-in is on by default and the first person to open a new instance is asked to create an administrator. This page covers that first run, the unattended alternative for automated installs, the small user-management panel, the fixed properties of the session cookie, and what actually changes if you turn authentication off. It ends with an honest account of a gap: there is no central place to manage credentials.

title: The sign-in rate limit
text: The sign-in endpoint is rate-limited to ten attempts per minute by default, in a fixed window partitioned by remote IP address, with nothing queued — an eleventh attempt in the same minute is refused with 429 rather than delayed. That throttles online password guessing without being tight enough to bother a person who mistyped twice. Two caveats. The partition is the remote IP, so behind a proxy that does not preserve the client address every caller shares one bucket and a single noisy client can lock out the rest. And the limit is per minute, not cumulative — it slows guessing rather than loc

title: Turning authentication off
text: Auth__Enabled=false removes the authentication middleware entirely. Every endpoint becomes anonymous — not merely the ones a signed-in user could reach, but all of them, including the capability toggle, the backup and restore endpoints and the Inline Code test endpoint. There is no sign-in and no first-run setup, and the interface does not gate itself behind a login screen. The admin-only gates become no-ops in that mode, which is consistent rather than a bug: there is no caller identity to check a role against, and every other endpoint is already open. title: Credentials: the honest gap
text: Credentials — the encrypted secrets that nodes reference for API keys, connection strings and passwords — have no management screen. There is no list of them, no way to browse or rename or delete one from the interface, and nothing under Settings that corresponds to them. This is a real gap, not something hidden in a submenu, and it is worth describing exactly so you do not spend time looking.

title: Configuration reference
text: Every setting Knotarium reads at startup, what it defaults to, and what changing it actually does. Most instances need none of this — the defaults are chosen so a fresh install works with no configuration at all. Reach for this page when you are running as a service, sharing data between installs, hardening an instance, or tracking down where your data went.

title: How settings are loaded
text: Settings come from several sources, each overriding the one before it: appsettings.json , next to the executable. appsettings.{Environment}.json — for example appsettings.Development.json . User secrets, in development builds only. Environment variables. Command-line arguments, which win over everything. Environment variables use a double underscore to express nesting. A setting written as Storage:DataDirectory in a JSON file becomes Storage__DataDirectory as an environment variable, because a colon is not a legal variable-name character on most systems. Both forms are listed for every setting

title: Where your data lives
text: This is the setting worth understanding before any other. One machine-wide directory holds everything that must survive an upgrade : the SQLite database, the encryption key that protects stored credentials, your workflow drafts, and the export folder. Everything that must survive an upgrade lives under one directory. Because the location is machine-wide rather than per-user, an interactive run and a Windows service running under a different account share the same database — which is what you want, and is the reason the default is %ProgramData% rather than a profile folder. title: The node editor
text: Knotarium ships a small authoring IDE for node packages, reached from Node Editor in the top navigation. It gives you a YAML manifest editor, a C# executor editor, a live rendering of the property form your manifest generates, and a sandboxed test runner whose result is a hard precondition for publishing. This page describes what each surface actually does — including several places where the editor is narrower than the manifest format it edits.

title: Opening it
text: The editor is a full-screen view, not a modal: choosing Node Editor replaces the canvas, and the Back button in its header returns you to whatever view you came from. There is no address you can bookmark — the view lives in React state like every other screen. Testing and publishing are administrator-only actions. Both POST /api/node-editor/test and POST /api/node-packages/publish check the caller's admin role before doing anything, because both end in compiling and running C# on the host. title: What the templates start you with
text: A declarative draft opens with a manifest declaring one string parameter named inputMessage , the logging capability, and success and error outputs. A compiled draft adds the http capability, renames the parameter to targetUrl , and fills Executor.cs with a complete INodeExecutor that reads the parameter, logs, and returns a NodeResult on the success output. Both templates set defaultTimeoutSeconds: 30 .

text: The manifest is re-parsed on every keystroke, and the result is not shown in the editor gutter. text: A passing test run is the only thing that opens the publish path, and it is remembered in memory. Publish Node refuses before it sends anything if the current session has no passing test result, with the message "Mandatory Gate Violated". That client-side check is courtesy; the server enforces the same rule independently. title: Signing is mandatory on publish
text: Publishing signs the package with the host's private key, so Security__PackageSigning__HostPrivateKeyBase64 must be configured and must decode to exactly 32 bytes. If it is missing, not valid base64, or the wrong length, the endpoint answers 500 with a message naming the setting. This is the single most common reason a first publish fails on a fresh instance — the key is optional for everything else, but not for this. See the Configuration reference .

title: Custom node packages
text: A node package is a manifest plus, optionally, an executor. The manifest declares what the node is called, which parameters it exposes, which sockets it has and which capabilities it needs; the executor is the C# that runs. This page is the reference for that format and for the three different routes a package can take into a running instance — the in-app editor, a signed install, and a compiled assembly dropped into a watched folder.

title: REST API
text: Everything the user interface does, it does over this API — there is no private channel and no second protocol. That makes the whole product scriptable, and it makes the API surface a security boundary worth understanding before you expose an instance to anything. This page enumerates the routes that exist, the authentication rules that apply to them, and the handful of responses that mean something other than "your request was wrong".

title: Base address and shape
text: Every route below is rooted at /api on the instance's own address — by default http://localhost:43120 . Requests and responses are JSON except where a route is explicitly noted as multipart upload or file download. There is no API version prefix and no published OpenAPI document for Knotarium's own API; the routes here are the contract. One route sits outside /api : GET /help serves this documentation and is anonymous, so the manual is readable from the sign-in screen.

title: Authentication
text: Authentication is a session cookie named kg_auth , issued by POST /api/auth/login . It is HttpOnly, SameSite Lax , HTTPS-only outside development, and slides forward on a seven-day expiry. There are no API keys and no bearer tokens: a script authenticates by logging in and keeping the cookie. With Auth__Enabled at its default of true , every endpoint requires an authenticated user unless it explicitly opts out. An unauthenticated call gets 401 and an authenticated-but-unauthorized one gets 403 — this is an API, so neither redirects to a login page. A subset of routes additionally requires the

title: The anonymous routes
text: Exactly five endpoints opt out of authentication, and each has its own reason: Route Why it is anonymous GET /api/auth/status The interface must be able to ask whether an admin exists before anyone can sign in. POST /api/auth/setup Creates the first administrator on an unconfigured instance. Only works while no accounts exist. POST /api/auth/login Obviously. Rate-limited — see below. POST /api/executions The machine-facing webhook trigger. Guarded by the arming switch, the workflow's enabled state, and an optional per-workflow secret rather than by a session. POST /api/executions/resume Resume

title: Rate limits
text: Two fixed-window limiters exist, both partitioned by remote IP address, both with no queue — past the limit the request is rejected immediately with 429 . POST /api/auth/login is limited by Security__RateLimit__LoginPerMinute , default 10 per minute, which is what blunts online password guessing. POST /api/executions and POST /api/executions/resume share a limit set by Security__RateLimit__AnonymousMachinePerMinute , default 60 per minute. A busy webhook source behind a single NAT address is the realistic reason to raise it. Nothing else is rate-limited, because everything else needs a session

title: Same-origin enforcement
text: Security__EnforceSameOrigin is Off by default . When enabled, an authenticated POST , PUT , PATCH or DELETE carrying an Origin header that matches neither this host nor a configured CORS origin is rejected with 403 and the body {"message":"Cross-origin state-changing request rejected."} . A request with no Origin header at all passes, which is why command-line clients are unaffected. It is off by default because a reverse proxy that rewrites Host produces false rejections. On a directly bound instance it is worth turning on: it is defence in depth over the SameSite cookie.

title: CORS
text: With Cors__AllowedOrigins empty — the default — any origin may call the API but credentials are refused, so a session cookie cannot be replayed from another origin. Listing origins switches to an allow-list that does permit credentials. Configure it only when a separate front-end origin genuinely needs to call this API; the bundled interface is same-origin in production and reaches the backend through the Vite proxy in development.

title: Keyboard shortcuts
text: The complete keyboard map. The editor carries an abbreviated version of this list built in — press ? anywhere on the canvas to see it — but that sheet covers the canvas only. This page also documents the keys bound inside the search palette, the run inspector, the code editor and the other panels, which the sheet does not list.

title: The cheat sheet built into the editor
text: Pressing ? toggles a panel titled Keyboard shortcuts over the canvas. It is rendered directly from the same shortcut table this page is written against, so it cannot drift from the handlers. Press ? again or Esc to close it, or use the close button in its corner. Opening the sheet is suppressed while the focus is in a text field, so typing a question mark into a node's property still types a question mark. Closing it is not suppressed: once the sheet is open, ? dismisses it from anywhere.

title: Ctrl and Command are interchangeable
text: Every shortcut on this page that shows Ctrl accepts Ctrl or ⌘ , on every platform. The handlers test for either modifier rather than branching on the operating system, so ⌘ Z works on a Mac keyboard plugged into Windows and Ctrl Z works on macOS. The platform difference is one of display , not behaviour. The in-app cheat sheet detects macOS and prints ⌘ ; everywhere else it prints Ctrl . Detection prefers the browser's modern platform hint and falls back to the older platform string and then the user-agent, so an unusual browser may show the Windows labels on a Mac — the keys themselves still

text: Keys Action Esc Close the editor. With unsaved changes this raises the confirmation sheet instead; a second Esc dismisses that sheet without closing. Leaving with unsaved changes asks for confirmation first.

title: Troubleshooting
text: Organised by what you observe rather than by which component is at fault. Almost every entry here has the same shape: something is refusing to happen quietly, because a secure default is doing its job. The messages quoted are the exact strings the application produces, so you can search this page for the text in front of you.

title: A scheduled workflow never fires
text: Three separate switches all have to be in the right position before a schedule produces a run, and none of them announces itself when it is not. Check them in this order. The runtime is disarmed. The switch in the header reads Disarmed . While it does, the scheduler and the pollers keep ticking but skip every evaluation, so there is no failed run to look at and nothing in the dead letter queue — the workflow simply does not appear to exist. A fresh instance starts disarmed on purpose, and so does one you have just been editing, because opening the canvas disarms it. Click the switch to arm it.

title: A webhook call is rejected
text: Inbound triggers go to a single anonymous endpoint, POST /api/executions , which names the target workflow in the request body. It applies seven checks in a fixed order and returns a different status for each, so the response tells you exactly which gate closed: Status Message What to do 401 Invalid or missing webhook secret. Send the secret in the X-Knotarium-Webhook-Secret header. This check is deliberately first so that an unauthorised caller cannot learn the instance's arming state. 409 Runtime is disarmed. Arm the runtime to allow external triggers. Arm the runtime from the header switch.

title: Webhook calls are rejected with an empty 429
text: Two different limits return 429 and they are easy to confuse. The queue-capacity rejection carries a JSON message naming the limit. The rate limit returns a bare 429 with no body at all — there is no rejection handler, so nothing explains itself. The anonymous machine-to-machine limit allows Security__RateLimit__AnonymousMachinePerMinute requests per minute, sixty by default, in a fixed one-minute window with no queueing, partitioned by the caller's IP address. It covers exactly two endpoints: the webhook trigger and run resumption. A burst of legitimate webhook traffic from one source address

title: The runtime disarmed itself
text: There are two mechanisms, and they behave differently enough that telling them apart matters. Opening the canvas editor disarms it. Every time you enter the editor from somewhere else, the runtime is disarmed. The reasoning is that design time should be safe time: a half-finished draft should not fire on a schedule while you are still moving nodes around. This writes the disarmed state to the database, so it survives a restart , and re-arming is always a deliberate click on the header switch. Nothing pops up to tell you it happened; the only hint in the interface is the tooltip on the toolbar'

title: My error workflow never runs
text: The global error handler is configured at Settings › Notifications . It is enqueued by an internal producer, which means it is never refused for queue depth — but it is a silent no-op when the workflow you nominated has no active version . An error workflow you drew and saved but never published will never run and will never complain. Publish it and set a version active.

title: A change appears to be ignored
My edits to the workflow have no effect
text: Nothing in Knotarium ever executes an unsaved draft. Not a trigger, and not the Run button. Pressing Run on the canvas activates whichever version is selected in the toolbar's version dropdown and then triggers the workflow. Your unsaved changes are not part of that version, so a run started immediately after an edit executes the code as it was when you last published. If the workflow has never been published at all, the run does not start and the toolbar reports Publish a version (Save & Publish) before running. The fix is always the same: press Save & Publish , which saves the draft, snapsho

title: A configuration change has no effect
text: There are four distinct reasons a setting can be edited correctly and still do nothing. The interface overrides the file. Several groups of settings are editable at runtime and are then stored in the database, where the stored value wins permanently over anything in appsettings.json or the environment. This applies to the sandbox ( Settings › Sandbox ), retention and the disk threshold ( Settings › Retention ), the capability policy ( Settings › Capabilities ), the file access policy ( Settings › File Access ), the AI provider ( Settings › AI Provider ) and the arming state. Change these in th

title: KG_AUTH_ENABLED or KG_ENCRYPTION_KEY has no effect
text: These are not application settings. They are shell variables interpolated by docker-compose.yml before the container ever starts, and the translation into real setting names happens entirely inside that file. Setting KG_AUTH_ENABLED=false on a zip install, a Windows service, a systemd unit or a plain docker run does nothing at all — and it fails silently, which is worse, because you are left believing sign-in is disabled when it is not. Outside Compose use the full names: Auth__Enabled , Security__Credentials__EncryptionKeyBase64 and Security__PackageSigning__HostPrivateKeyBase64 .

title: A node is refused at run time
A File Read or File Write node is denied
text: File access is deny-by-default: a fresh instance permits nothing, and every path must be granted explicitly. The node fails with File read failed: or File write failed: followed by the specific reason, and carries the error code FileAccessDenied . The reasons distinguish four different situations: Reason Meaning … is not permitted (nothing is granted yet). An administrator must grant it under Settings → File Access. The policy is empty. All refusals start with Outbound egress denied . The variants tell you which rule fired: Message Rule Outbound egress denied for local host '…'. localhost and any name ending in .local or .internal . This one is unconditional — turning off DenyPrivateNetworks does not lift it. Outbound egress denied for private or loopback address '…'. title: Runs queue up or are refused
text: Four runs execute at once by default and the rest wait, so a backlog is normal rather than a fault. Refusal only starts when the queue reaches Execution__MaxQueueDepth , one thousand by default, at which point new starts get 429 with the message Execution queue is at capacity (1000 pending runs). Retry later. Which starts are refused is not obvious and is worth knowing before you raise any limits: Refused: manual runs, inbound webhook calls, and firing a schedule by hand from the editor. title: The provider is not configured
text: Every AI node fails with the same sentence until a provider is set up: The AI provider is not configured. Choose a provider, model, and API-key credential in Settings → AI Provider. The configuration is only considered complete when all three are present: a recognised vendor, a non-blank model name, and a credential reference. Setting the vendor and leaving the model blank produces this same message, which reads as though nothing was configured at all. The supported vendors are Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure OpenAI and Gemini. An administrator can enable it under Settings → Capabilities. That advice cannot currently be followed Settings › Capabilities renders only two toggles, for inline code and database access. There is no toggle for the AI Agent capability, even though the backend accepts it as switchable and the node enforces it. title: Saved credentials cannot be decrypted after a move or restore
text: Knotarium.db stores credentials encrypted; .credential-key in the same data directory is what decrypts them. Copying the database without the key file is the single most damaging mistake available in this product, and the way it fails is what makes it dangerous. It does not fail at startup. Finding no key file, the application generates a new random one and carries on. The instance starts cleanly, the credentials are all still listed by name, and everything looks intact. Only when a workflow actually resolves a credential does it fail, with an authentication-tag mismatch from the cryptography

title: Upgrading left the workflows or the database behind
text: Older builds kept workflow drafts in the per-user %APPDATA%\Knotarium folder. On every non-development startup the application looks there and moves what it finds into the current data directory. What it moves is narrow: Draft .json files from %APPDATA%\Knotarium\workflows\ , not recursively. groups.json . It moves nothing else . Not the database, not the credential key, not the export folder. If your previous installation kept Knotarium.db next to the executable, the new version starts with an empty database and the old one sits where it always was. Copy it and its .credential-key into the da

title: Startup fails because authentication is disabled
text: If Auth__Enabled is false while any configured binding is not a loopback address, startup aborts on purpose with: Authentication is disabled (Auth:Enabled=false) but the server is configured to bind a non-loopback address (…). In no-auth mode every endpoint is anonymous, so this would expose an unauthenticated remote-code-execution surface. Bind loopback only (e.g. http://127.0.0.1:PORT), enable authentication (Auth:Enabled=true), or set Security:AllowUnauthenticatedNonLoopback=true to accept the risk (e.g. behind a trusted reverse proxy). The guard inspects both the aggregate URL setting — wh

title: Startup fails on the audit chain
text: The audit log is hash-chained and the chain is verified during startup; a chain that does not verify aborts the launch rather than starting with a log that can no longer be trusted. This is normally a symptom of a partially restored or hand-edited database. Note that enabling audit retention deliberately rewrites the chain to re-anchor the surviving entries, so older entries can no longer be checked against the original chain — that is expected, not corruption.

title: Where to find the logs
text: Application logging is console-only, one line of compact JSON per event, written to standard output. There is no log file and no rolling policy — do not go looking for a logs folder, there is not one. The log level is fixed in code at information, with database logging held down to warnings, and cannot be changed through configuration. title: Glossary
text: Every term this manual uses with a meaning specific to Knotarium, defined in one or two sentences and linked to the page that covers it properly. Where the interface and the code disagree about a word — and in a few places they do — both are given, because you will meet both.

title: A
text: Active version — the one published version of a workflow that actually executes. It is recorded separately from the versions themselves, in a pointer with an append-only activation history, and every trigger resolves through it. A workflow with published versions but none set active cannot be triggered. Arming — the instance-wide switch in the header that gates every automatic trigger. While disarmed, schedules and pollers keep ticking but skip their work, inbound webhook calls are refused, and only manual runs execute. See Runtime arming . Audit log — an append-only, hash-chained record of pr

title: B
text: Backup — a whole-instance archive, extension .kgbak , protected either by a passphrase or by this server's own credential key. A server-key backup restores only on the host that created it and only while that host's key is unchanged. See Backup and restore . Bundle — a distributable archive, extension .kgbundle , holding several workflows together with the node packages they depend on. It carries both an authoring manifest and a resolved lock file recording exact versions, hashes and trust levels, which is verified at install. See Bundles .

title: C
text: Capability — a named privilege that a node declares it needs and that an administrator must grant instance-wide before any node holding it will run. Three are switchable — code execution, database access and the AI agent — and all of them are off by default , an unset policy meaning everything is denied. See Capabilities . Condition — a node that evaluates a logical expression tree and routes the run down its true or false output port. It has a dedicated full-screen editor rather than a text field, because a condition is a structured tree and not a string. See Conditions and branching . Correl

title: D
text: Dead letter — the triage view listing every run that ended in failure, so that failures are worked through deliberately rather than scrolled past. Discarding a run from it marks it handled; it is not a deletion. See Dead letter queue . Diagnostics — the compiler's findings about the graph you are currently drawing: missing sub-flow references, unreachable nodes, incomplete conditions and the like. These are design-time messages about the workflow, not run-time errors and not application logs. See Diagnostics . Discarded — the state a failed run moves to when you triage it away in the dead lett

title: E
text: Edge — a connection from a named output port on one node to a named input port on another. Edges carry the flow of control and the data together, which is why deleting a node also deletes every edge touching it. See Core concepts . Egress policy — the rules governing what the instance may connect out to, applied to every outbound request the engine makes and re-checked on every physical connection including each redirect. By default it refuses private, loopback and link-local destinations. See Security model . Error workflow — a workflow nominated to run whenever any other workflow fails, seed

title: F
text: Failure alert — the per-workflow routing of failure notifications, which can inherit the instance default, be switched off, or name its own channel. See Error handling and alerts . File access policy — the allow-list governing the File Read and File Write nodes. It is deny-by-default and empty on a fresh instance; grants are made one directory at a time, apply recursively to everything beneath, and are scoped to reading, writing or both. See File access .

title: G
text: Group — two unrelated things share this word. On the dashboard a group is a folder that organises workflows; on the canvas a Group node is an inert visual container that frames a region of the graph and moves its members with it. See The canvas editor .

title: J
text: Journal — the append-only event log of a single run, recording what each node received, what it produced and what the variables looked like at each point. It is the system of record from which a run's status is reconstructed, and it is what makes replay, time travel and crash recovery possible. See Runs and the inspector .

title: M
text: Manual decision — the resolution a person supplies when a run was interrupted part way through an external effect and the system cannot safely determine whether that effect happened. Until it is answered, the node holds the run rather than guessing.

title: N
text: Node — one step in a workflow: an HTTP request, a branch, a database query, a log line. Every node is an instance of a node type whose behaviour, parameters and ports are declared by a manifest. See How to read this reference . Node package — the registry entry for a node type: a manifest declaring its parameters, ports, capabilities, timeout and retry policy, plus optionally a compiled assembly implementing it. Around thirty-five first-party types are built in; further ones are installed or published into the database. See Custom node packages . Node tier — how a node type's behaviour is supp

title: O
text: OpenAPI spec — an imported API description whose operations become callable nodes. Importing one is a distinct feature from the workflow importer, and lives under its own nav entry. See Importing OpenAPI . Output port — a named socket a node emits from. Ports are semantic rather than positional: a Condition has true and false , an HTTP Request has success and error , and a plain data node has result . Some node types generate their ports from their configuration instead of declaring them in a manifest.

title: P
text: Pinned output — a sample payload frozen onto a node so that downstream nodes can be built and tested without re-executing what precedes them. A pin travels with the draft into the published version but is honoured only on manual runs; automatic runs ignore it. See The canvas editor . Polling trigger — a trigger that fetches a source on an interval and starts a run only when something has changed, using an ETag, a last-modified header, a content hash or a cursor in the response. See Trigger nodes . Publishing — compiling the draft and, if it compiles, snapshotting it as a new immutable numbered

title: R
text: Recovery mode — whether a node type retries automatically after a failure or fails immediately. It is declared per node type and follows from the side-effect kind: nodes whose effects are safe to repeat retry, and nodes whose effects are not do not. Replay — starting a new run seeded from a finished run's state at a chosen node, so that everything upstream is reused and that node onward re-executes. It is not a re-run from the start. You choose which version to replay against and whether to mock side effects. See Runs and the inspector . Resource locator — a parameter whose choices are loaded

title: S
text: Sandbox — the isolation applied to user-authored C#, meaning the Inline Code node and compiled custom packages. It runs that code either inside the main process or in pooled worker processes with memory, CPU and lifetime limits imposed by the operating system. See Sandbox . Schedule — a persisted cron trigger attached to a workflow. Each individual firing is recorded separately as it is claimed, which is what stops two firings of the same occurrence from producing two runs. See Triggers . Side-effect kind — whether a node's effect is safe to repeat. This single property drives two visible beha

title: T
text: Template — a shareable archive of one workflow, extension .kgtpl , stripped of secrets and carrying authoring metadata, declared credential slots and install-time parameters. Templates come either from a read-only built-in gallery or from the library of ones saved on this instance. See Templates . Template parameter — a non-secret blank the template's author deliberately left for whoever installs it, referenced inside the workflow as {{ param:<Key> }} . Time travel — stepping backwards and forwards through a finished run, one node at a time, seeing that node's inputs, outputs and the variable

title: V
text: Variable — a named value scoped to a run, written by the Set Variable nodes and read through {{ $variables.… }} . The editor's Workflow variables panel additionally tracks which node produces each one and which nodes consume it, so an unresolved variable is visible before you run anything. Credentials are a separate, encrypted store and are not variables. See Variables . Version — an immutable numbered snapshot of a workflow, created by publishing, by restoring an older version, or by importing one. A version that fails to compile is never created. See Versions and publishing .

title: W
text: Webhook secret — an optional per-workflow shared secret sent in a request header by an inbound caller. It is checked before anything else about the request, so that an unauthorised caller cannot learn even whether the runtime is armed. A workflow with no secret configured accepts anonymous calls. See Triggers . Work item — a durable queue row that brings a parked run back to life: resuming it after a delay or an event, retrying a failed node, or delivering a manual decision. It is the reason a suspended run survives a restart. Workflow — the graph you draw, and the unit you save, publish, shar
